q: Ron and Sue inherit a duplex as tenants in common. They split the rent equally and each pays half of every repair bill. Under RUPA § 202, which of the following statements is true?
o: They are partners, because they share the rental profits equally.
They are not partners merely because they co-own property and share its returns.
They are partners, because they share the duplex's expenses as well as its income.
They are not partners, because they never filed anything with the state.
They are not partners, because neither of them intended to form a partnership.
oe: Profit sharing raises a presumption only when the profits come from a business; the statute singles out co-owned property and its returns as not enough by themselves.

Correct. RUPA § 202(c)(1)–(2): co-ownership of property does not by itself establish a partnership, even if the co-owners share profits made by its use, and sharing gross returns does not by itself establish one either. Nothing suggests they carry on a business as co-owners.
Sharing expenses on co-owned property is still just co-ownership; it does not show co-owners carrying on a business for profit.
Right result, wrong reason. A general partnership needs no filing at all; if they were carrying on a business as co-owners, they would be partners without one.
Intent to be partners is not required: a partnership forms "whether or not the persons intend to form a partnership" (§ 202(a)).
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Co-ownership is not enough

q: Which of the following can amount to a principal's ratification of an agent's unauthorized contract?
o: Knowingly accepting the benefits of the contract.
Suing the third party to enforce the contract.
Staying silent, with knowledge of the material facts, when a reasonable person in the principal's position would object.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Accepting benefits with knowledge of the material facts is the most common form of implied ratification (R3d § 4.01).
True. Ratification may be shown by conduct that is justifiable only if the principal assents, and suing to enforce the deal is such conduct.
True. Silence ratifies where the principal knows the facts and has a duty to speak or disaffirm (compare Ercanbrack: silence can't ratify when the principal knows nothing).
Incomplete. Suing to enforce the contract is also ratifying conduct.
Correct. Ratification can be express or implied, and accepting benefits, suing to enforce, and silence where there is a duty to speak can all show the principal's assent.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ways to ratify

q: Under the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA) in the statutory supplement, a member of a member-managed LLC:
o: May demand a distribution from the LLC at any time before it dissolves.
Becomes personally liable for LLC debts if the members stop holding meetings.
Owes the LLC and the other members the duties of loyalty and care.
Is an agent of the LLC solely because she is a member.
None of the above.
oe: There is no right to interim distributions (§ 404(b)); the members decide whether to make them.
ULLCA § 304: failing to observe formalities is not a ground for imposing personal liability on members or managers.
Correct. In a member-managed LLC the members owe the § 409 duties of loyalty and care, plus the obligation of good faith and fair dealing.
ULLCA § 301(a): a member is not an agent of the LLC solely by reason of being a member. Authority comes from agency law or a filed statement of authority.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Member of a member-managed LLC

q: A principal is generally not liable for the torts of an independent contractor. Which of the following is NOT an exception to that rule?
o: The principal paid the contractor a fixed price for the job rather than an hourly wage.
The work was inherently dangerous unless special precautions were taken.
The principal owed a nondelegable duty to the injured person.
The principal carelessly hired a contractor that it knew, or should have known, was incompetent for the job.
The principal retained control over how the work was done.
oe: Correct: this is not an exception. Payment by the job is one of the R2d § 220 factors suggesting that the worker is an independent contractor in the first place; it makes the principal less likely to be liable, not more.
An exception (Majestic Realty: demolition on a crowded downtown block).
An exception (Kleeman v. Rheingold: a lawyer's duty to have process served properly).
An exception, and a form of direct liability for negligent selection (R3d § 7.05).
An exception. A principal that keeps control over the work answers for the harm that control produces.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Independent contractors: not an exception

q: A partnership agreement governed by the RUPA (1997) provides: "No partner may withdraw from the partnership before December 31, 2035." In 2028, Pia gives her partners written notice that she is withdrawing. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Pia's withdrawal automatically dissolves the partnership.
Pia's withdrawal is rightful, because every partner has the right to withdraw at any time.
Pia's withdrawal has no effect, because the agreement validly took away her power to withdraw.
Pia is dissociated, but her withdrawal is wrongful and she is liable for the damages it causes.
None of the above.
oe: Under RUPA, dissociation does not necessarily dissolve the firm. A partnership for a term dissolves after a wrongful dissociation only if at least half of the remaining partners vote within 90 days to wind it up (§ 801(2)(A)).
Every partner has the power to withdraw, not always the right. Here leaving breaches an express term.
The power to dissociate cannot be eliminated by agreement (§ 105(c)); the agreement can only make its exercise wrongful (and may require that notice be written).

Correct. A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will (§ 602(a)), but withdrawal that breaches an express provision of the agreement is wrongful (§ 602(b)(1)), and the wrongdoer is liable for damages (§ 602(c)).
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Power vs. right to withdraw

q: Three software engineers plan to start a business. They want (1) no personal liability for the business's debts, (2) a single layer of income tax, and (3) the freedom to set up management by private agreement rather than through a board of directors. Which business form best meets all three goals?
o: A general partnership.
A sole proprietorship.
A limited liability company (LLC).
A corporation.
A limited partnership in which all three are general partners.
oe: Pass-through tax and flexible management, yes, but every partner is personally liable for partnership obligations (RUPA § 306(a)).
A sole proprietorship has a single owner, and it does not separate the owner's personal assets from the business's liabilities.
Correct. An LLC combines a full liability shield for its members with pass-through taxation, and as a "creature of contract," its operating agreement sets up management as the members choose.
Limited liability, yes, but shareholders elect a board that hires the officers, and a regular corporation is taxed at the entity level as well.
General partners of an LP are personally liable for its obligations, and an LP must also have at least one limited partner.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Choosing an entity

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gina, Hal, and Ivy are partners in Keystone Masonry, a general partnership that builds stone walls and patios. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall continue for eight years from the date of this agreement." "Profits and losses shall be shared equally." "A new partner may be admitted by majority vote of the partners." Hal handles the firm's trucks and equipment; Ivy prepares bids.

While driving the partnership's dump truck to a job site, Hal negligently strikes a cyclist, Nate, causing $300,000 in damages. The partnership's assets are worth $120,000. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Only Hal is liable, because he alone was negligent, and partners are not liable for one another's torts.
All three partners are jointly and severally liable, subject to exhausting partnership assets first.
The partnership is liable, but Gina and Ivy are liable only up to the amount of their capital contributions.
Gina and Ivy are liable only if they ratified Hal's driving or took part in it.
None of the above.
oe: Hal is liable for his own tort, but the partnership is liable for a partner's tort committed in the ordinary course of its business, and the partners are liable for partnership obligations.

Correct. The partnership answers for a partner's tort in the ordinary course (RUPA § 305), the partners are jointly and severally liable for its obligations (§ 306(a)), and a judgment creditor generally must first exhaust the partnership's assets before levying on a partner's personal assets (§ 307(d)). Nate may of course sue Hal directly as the tortfeasor.
That describes a limited partner or LLC member. Partners in a general partnership have unlimited personal liability.
Their liability arises from their status as partners (§ 306(a)), not from participation or ratification.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Tort claims against partners

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gina, Hal, and Ivy are partners in Keystone Masonry, a general partnership that builds stone walls and patios. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall continue for eight years from the date of this agreement." "Profits and losses shall be shared equally." "A new partner may be admitted by majority vote of the partners." Hal handles the firm's trucks and equipment; Ivy prepares bids.

In Year 3, Hal announces that he is withdrawing from Keystone Masonry to start his own company. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Hal is wrongfully dissociated and owes damages, but the partnership does not automatically dissolve.
Hal's withdrawal is rightful, because he gave his partners notice before leaving and owes them nothing.
The partnership automatically dissolves, because it is a partnership for a term.
Hal cannot withdraw at all before the eight-year term ends, because the agreement fixes the term.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Withdrawal by express will before the end of an agreed term is wrongful (§ 602(b)(2)(i)), and the wrongdoer owes damages (§ 602(c)). Under RUPA, his dissociation leads to a buyout unless the remaining partners act to wind up (§§ 603, 801(2)).
Notice makes a withdrawal effective, not rightful. Leaving before the end of the term is wrongful.
That was the UPA (1914) rule. RUPA separates dissociation from dissolution.
He has the power to withdraw at any time (§ 602(a)); he lacks only the right.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Wrongful dissociation in a term partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gina, Hal, and Ivy are partners in Keystone Masonry, a general partnership that builds stone walls and patios. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall continue for eight years from the date of this agreement." "Profits and losses shall be shared equally." "A new partner may be admitted by majority vote of the partners." Hal handles the firm's trucks and equipment; Ivy prepares bids.

Sixty days after Hal leaves, Gina tells Ivy that she wants to wind up the business. Ivy wants to keep it going. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership dissolves, because at least half of the remaining partners chose to wind up within 90 days.
The partnership continues, because Gina cannot force a dissolution before the eight-year term ends.
The partnership continues, because a majority of the remaining partners must vote to wind it up.
The partnership dissolves only if Hal agrees.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. After a wrongful dissociation from a term partnership, the firm dissolves if, within 90 days, at least half of the remaining partners express their will to wind up (§ 801(2)(A)). Gina is half of the two remaining partners.
§ 801(2)(A) is exactly the way a term partnership can be dissolved early after a wrongful dissociation.
The statute asks for "at least half," not a majority, of the remaining partners.
Hal, the wrongful dissociator, has no vote on whether the others wind up.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Voting to wind up (§ 801(2)(A))

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gina, Hal, and Ivy are partners in Keystone Masonry, a general partnership that builds stone walls and patios. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall continue for eight years from the date of this agreement." "Profits and losses shall be shared equally." "A new partner may be admitted by majority vote of the partners." Hal handles the firm's trucks and equipment; Ivy prepares bids.

Assume instead that Gina and Ivy continue the business and buy out Hal. They worry that Hal, who still knows all of the firm's suppliers, will keep ordering stone on the partnership's account. Which step would protect the partnership from such orders most quickly?
o: Amending the partnership agreement to strip Hal of authority.
Doing nothing, because a dissociated partner can never bind the partnership.
Filing a statement of dissociation, which cuts off Hal's power to bind on the day it is filed.
Notifying each supplier directly that Hal is no longer a partner.
None of the above.
oe: Hal is no longer a partner, and an amendment between the remaining partners gives outsiders no notice.
For two years a dissociated partner can bind the firm to third parties who lack notice and reasonably believe he is still a partner (§ 702).
A filed statement of dissociation works, but non-partners are deemed to have notice of it only 90 days after it is filed (§§ 103(d), 704). It is not the fastest protection.

Correct. A dissociated partner binds the partnership only if the other party does not know or have notice of the dissociation and reasonably believes he is still a partner (§ 702). A supplier that has been told cannot meet that test, starting immediately.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Cutting off a departed partner's authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gina, Hal, and Ivy are partners in Keystone Masonry, a general partnership that builds stone walls and patios. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall continue for eight years from the date of this agreement." "Profits and losses shall be shared equally." "A new partner may be admitted by majority vote of the partners." Hal handles the firm's trucks and equipment; Ivy prepares bids.

Before Hal leaves, Gina and Ivy vote to admit Jo as a partner over Hal's objection. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Jo is a partner, and she is personally liable for every partnership obligation, including those incurred before she joined.
Jo is a partner, and her capital contribution is protected from creditors whose claims arose before she joined.
Jo's admission is invalid, because admitting a partner always requires the consent of all partners.
Hal is dissociated, because he was outvoted on a fundamental matter.
None of the above.
oe: § 306(b) protects an incoming partner's personal assets from pre-admission obligations.
Wrong. § 306(b) protects only Jo's personal assets from pre-admission obligations; whatever she contributes to the partnership is available to all of its creditors.
Unanimity is the default rule, and the partnership agreement may change it. Admission is not among the § 105(c) terms the agreement cannot vary.
Being outvoted is not a dissociation event, and adding a partner does not dissociate anyone.

Correct. Jo is validly admitted, because the agreement lets a majority admit a partner (RUPA § 402's unanimity rule is only a default). She is not personally liable for obligations incurred before her admission, but her contribution is at risk (§ 306(b)). None of A–D states this correctly.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Admitting a new partner

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marlowe, a wealthy art collector, wants to buy paintings from local galleries without the galleries raising their prices. She hires Nico to buy for her and tells him to buy in his own name and never mention her. She also gives him a written instruction: "Do not pay more than $50,000 for any one painting, and do not buy on credit." Over the past year Nico has bought several paintings for cash from Orchard Gallery, which believes he is a private collector buying for himself.

Contrary to Marlowe's instruction, Nico buys a $40,000 painting from Orchard Gallery on 30-day credit. Before paying, Nico disappears. Orchard then learns that Nico was buying for Marlowe. Can Orchard recover the price from Marlowe?
o: No, because Nico violated an express instruction, so he had no actual authority to buy on credit.
No, because Orchard did not know Marlowe existed, so Nico could not have had apparent authority.
Yes; an undisclosed principal cannot rely on secret limits on her agent's usual authority.
Yes, but only if Marlowe ratifies the purchase.
None of the above.
oe: Lack of actual authority is the premise, not the end, of the analysis. The undisclosed-principal rules bind Marlowe anyway.
True that apparent authority is missing, since Marlowe made no manifestation to Orchard. But that is exactly the gap Watteau and R3d § 2.06 fill.

Correct. This is Watteau v. Fenwick: an undisclosed principal answers for acts within the authority usually given such an agent, despite secret limits. R3d § 2.06(2) keeps the result: an undisclosed principal may not rely on instructions that reduce the agent's authority below what a third party would reasonably believe the agent had if the principal were disclosed.
Ratification is one route, but Marlowe is bound here without it.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal and secret limits

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marlowe, a wealthy art collector, wants to buy paintings from local galleries without the galleries raising their prices. She hires Nico to buy for her and tells him to buy in his own name and never mention her. She also gives him a written instruction: "Do not pay more than $50,000 for any one painting, and do not buy on credit." Over the past year Nico has bought several paintings for cash from Orchard Gallery, which believes he is a private collector buying for himself.

Orchard sues Nico for the unpaid $40,000. Nico argues that he was only Marlowe's agent. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Nico is liable only if he acted without any authority at all.
Nico is liable, because an agent for an undisclosed principal is a party to the contract.
Nico is not liable, because Marlowe is now bound on the contract and only one of them can be liable.
Nico is not liable, because he can escape liability by now disclosing Marlowe.
None of the above.
oe: An agent for an undisclosed principal is a party to the contract even when he acts with full authority.

Correct. When the principal is undisclosed, the agent is a party to the contract (R3d § 6.03). The third party believed it was dealing with Nico alone, so he cannot step aside by naming Marlowe later.
Both may be liable: the agent as a party and the undisclosed principal on the contract.
Disclosure after the fact does not release an agent who contracted as a party.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Agent of an undisclosed principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marlowe, a wealthy art collector, wants to buy paintings from local galleries without the galleries raising their prices. She hires Nico to buy for her and tells him to buy in his own name and never mention her. She also gives him a written instruction: "Do not pay more than $50,000 for any one painting, and do not buy on credit." Over the past year Nico has bought several paintings for cash from Orchard Gallery, which believes he is a private collector buying for himself.

Nico agrees, in his own name, to buy a $70,000 painting from Orchard, which is $20,000 over Marlowe's limit. When Marlowe hears about it, she decides she wants the painting. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Marlowe may ratify only if Orchard consents.
Under the Restatement (Third) she may ratify, though the Restatement (Second) would not allow it.
Marlowe may ratify the purchase at $50,000, her stated limit, and reject the excess.
Neither Restatement lets an undisclosed principal ratify, because the third party never relied on her.
None of the above.
oe: Ratification is the principal's unilateral act; the third party's consent is not required (though a third party that has already withdrawn cannot be bound).
Correct. The R2d allowed only disclosed and unidentified (partially disclosed) principals to ratify; the R3d lets any principal on whose behalf the agent acted ratify, including an undisclosed one.
There is no partial ratification. A principal must affirm the entire transaction or none of it (R3d § 4.07).
That was the R2d rule only; the R3d changed it.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification by an undisclosed principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marlowe, a wealthy art collector, wants to buy paintings from local galleries without the galleries raising their prices. She hires Nico to buy for her and tells him to buy in his own name and never mention her. She also gives him a written instruction: "Do not pay more than $50,000 for any one painting, and do not buy on credit." Over the past year Nico has bought several paintings for cash from Orchard Gallery, which believes he is a private collector buying for himself.

While shopping for Marlowe, Nico learns of a rare painting that she has hunted for years. He buys it with his own money for $60,000 and then offers to sell it to Marlowe for $90,000, without telling her that he is the seller. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Nico breached his duty not to deal with Marlowe as an adverse party without disclosing the facts.
If Marlowe buys the painting, she may recover the profit Nico made from the resale.
Nico committed no breach, because he bought the painting with his own funds.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. An agent may not deal with the principal as, or on behalf of, an adverse party in a transaction connected with the agency (R3d § 8.03) unless the principal consents after full disclosure.
True. Profits an agent makes through his position belong to the principal; disgorgement removes his incentive to breach (R3d § 8.02; General Automotive v. Singer).
Using his own money does not cure the conflict. He learned of the opportunity through the agency and then dealt with his principal secretly.
Correct. Nico secretly dealt as an adverse party, and Marlowe may make him give up the profit.
C is wrong; a fiduciary cannot avoid his duty of loyalty by using his own funds.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Dealing as an adverse party

q: Paula hires Quentin, a real estate broker, to sell her house. With Paula's permission, Quentin hires Rae, a licensed associate in his office, to hold open houses. Rae is best described as:
o: A coagent, because she and Quentin both work for Paula.
A gratuitous agent, because Paula does not pay her.
A subagent, who owes fiduciary duties to Paula.
Paula's general agent.
No one's agent, because Paula never spoke to her.
oe: Coagents are agents appointed by the same principal. Rae was appointed by Quentin.
Who pays her does not decide her status, and nothing suggests she works for free.

Correct. A subagent is appointed by an agent, with authority to do so, to perform functions the agent has undertaken for the principal; the appointing agent answers to the principal for the subagent, and the subagent is the principal's fiduciary too (R3d §§ 1.04(8), 3.15).
Rae was brought in for a limited task, and by Quentin, not Paula.
Paula's consent to Quentin's hiring a helper is enough; direct contact is not required.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Subagents

q: A partnership files a statement of partnership authority providing that only partner Uma may transfer the partnership's real property, and it records a certified copy in the county land records. Partner Vic then signs a deed conveying partnership land to Wynn, who never checks the records. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Wynn is deemed to know of the limit, so Vic's deed does not bind the partnership.
The statement is void, because the RUPA does not allow partners to limit one another's authority.
Wynn takes good title, because every partner is an agent of the partnership for the ordinary course of business.
Wynn takes good title, because a filed limitation on a partner's authority is never notice to third parties.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Filed limits on authority generally are not notice to third parties, but a limitation on authority to transfer real property is, once a certified copy is recorded in the office for recording transfers of that property (§§ 103(d), 303).
Partners may limit authority among themselves; § 303 lets them publicize grants and limits.
Agency under § 301 yields to a limit the third party is deemed to know.
That is the general rule, but recorded limits on authority to transfer real property are the exception.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Recorded limit on real property

q: A bank's loan officer, using the bank's letterhead and sitting in his bank office, persuades a customer to buy a "bank-guaranteed" certificate that does not exist and keeps the money. Under the Restatement (Third) of Agency, the bank's liability to the customer is best based on:
o: No theory, because fraud for one's own benefit is always outside the scope of employment.
Vicarious liability, because the officer committed the tort with apparent authority.
Negligent supervision only.
Ratification, which is required before a principal is liable for an agent's fraud.
None of the above.
oe: Scope of employment is not the only route. A tort committed with apparent authority makes the principal liable even if the agent served only himself.

Correct. R3d § 7.08: a principal is vicariously liable for an agent's tort when actions taken by the agent with apparent authority constitute the tort, as with fraud or misrepresentation that the third party believes is the principal's own dealing.
Direct liability for negligent supervision is possible if facts show it, but it is not needed when the agent acted with apparent authority.
Ratification is one basis for liability, not a prerequisite.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Torts committed with apparent authority

q: Zed, a partner in a RUPA general partnership, wants to buy the partnership's used delivery van for his own use. Which of the following could protect Zed from a claim that he breached the duty of loyalty?
o: All of the partners authorize the sale after full disclosure of all material facts.
The partnership agreement, in a provision that is not manifestly unreasonable, permits partners to buy partnership equipment.
Zed proves that the transaction was fair to the partnership.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. § 409(f): all the partners may authorize or ratify a specific transaction, after full disclosure, that would otherwise breach loyalty.
True. The agreement may identify specific types of activities that do not violate loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable (§ 105(d)).
True. Fairness is a defense to a claim of dealing with the partnership as an adverse party (§ 409(g)).
Incomplete. Fairness is also a statutory defense to self-dealing.
Correct. Advance authorization, a permitting clause in the agreement, and proof of fairness can each defeat a self-dealing claim.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Protecting a self-dealing partner

q: A partnership agreement provides that either partner may name a price, and the other partner must then either buy the first partner's interest at that price or sell his own interest at that price. Which of the following statements best describes this clause?
o: The offering partner has a reason to name a fair price, since the other may buy at it.
The clause is unenforceable, because the RUPA requires an Article 7 buyout at going-concern value.
The partner who receives the offer must sell at the named price.
The price is set by a court-appointed appraiser if the partners disagree.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The first mover sets the price, but the other side chooses whether to buy or sell at it, so naming a low price risks having to sell cheap, and naming a high price risks having to buy dear.
The § 701 buyout rules are defaults the partners may replace by agreement.
The recipient chooses to buy or to sell; that choice is what disciplines the price.
This clause avoids appraisal; the named price controls.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Shotgun buy-sell clause

q: A law firm general partnership becomes a limited liability partnership (LLP). Which of the following statements is true?
o: The firm becomes an LLP as soon as the partners sign an agreement calling the firm an LLP.
A partner is not personally liable for an obligation the firm incurs while it is an LLP solely because she is a partner.
A partner remains personally liable for her own malpractice.
B and C.
A, B and C.
oe: False. LLP status requires filing a statement of qualification with the state (RUPA § 901).
True. RUPA § 306(c).
True. The LLP shield covers liability that arises from partner status, not liability for one's own torts.
Correct. The shield protects partners from the firm's obligations but not from their own wrongdoing, and it takes a filing to get it.
A is wrong; signing an agreement is not enough without the filing.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Limited liability partnerships

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Coastline Plumbing, Inc. employs Drew as a plumber. Drew drives a Coastline van, is paid by the hour, and must follow Coastline's dispatch schedule and safety manual. Coastline's written rules forbid employees to use the van for personal errands and forbid them to argue with customers about bills; billing disputes must be sent to the office.

Between two jobs, Drew drives six blocks out of his way to pick up lunch and, on the way, rear-ends Elle's car. Is Coastline likely liable to Elle?
o: No, because company rules forbid personal errands in the van.
No, because getting lunch serves only Drew's own purposes.
Yes, because a short lunch stop between jobs is only a detour.
Yes, but only because Coastline owns the van.
None of the above.
oe: Forbidden conduct can still be within the scope of employment (R2d § 230).
Eating during the workday is incidental to the job. The question is whether the deviation was so great that he abandoned the employer's business, and a six-block detour is not.

Correct. A brief, foreseeable deviation is a "detour," not a "frolic." Drew was still on duty, in the employer's van, between assigned jobs (R2d §§ 228–229); under R3d § 7.07 this was not an independent course of conduct serving no purpose of Coastline.
Ownership of the vehicle does not by itself make the employer vicariously liable; scope of employment does.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Detour

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Coastline Plumbing, Inc. employs Drew as a plumber. Drew drives a Coastline van, is paid by the hour, and must follow Coastline's dispatch schedule and safety manual. Coastline's written rules forbid employees to use the van for personal errands and forbid them to argue with customers about bills; billing disputes must be sent to the office.

After finishing his last job of the day, Drew drives the van 40 miles in the opposite direction from his home and the shop to attend his cousin's birthday party, and he crashes on the way. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Coastline is liable, because violating a company rule never takes conduct outside the scope of employment.
Coastline is probably not vicariously liable, because Drew had left on a frolic of his own.
Coastline is liable, because it furnished the van.
Coastline is liable under Bushey, because driving is a risk characteristic of a plumbing business.
None of the above.
oe: Rule violations don't automatically take conduct outside scope, but here the problem is that Drew had abandoned the employer's business entirely.
Correct. A long trip, after work, for a purely personal purpose is a frolic, outside the scope of employment (R2d § 228; R3d § 7.07(2)).
Furnishing the instrumentality is one § 229 factor, but it does not override a complete departure from the employer's business.
Even Bushey's enterprise-risk approach excludes conduct arising from the employee's purely personal life, like a family party 40 miles away.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Frolic

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Coastline Plumbing, Inc. employs Drew as a plumber. Drew drives a Coastline van, is paid by the hour, and must follow Coastline's dispatch schedule and safety manual. Coastline's written rules forbid employees to use the van for personal errands and forbid them to argue with customers about bills; billing disputes must be sent to the office.

A customer, Finn, refuses to pay and stands in front of Drew's toolbox to stop him from leaving with it. Drew shoves Finn aside to get his tools back, and Finn is hurt. Is Coastline likely liable to Finn?
o: Yes, because the shove grew out of his work, even though it broke company rules.
Yes, but only if Coastline later ratifies the shove.
No, because an intentional tort is never within the scope of employment.
No, because Coastline's rules forbade arguing with customers.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Drew used force while trying to finish the job and retrieve the employer's tools, so his act was at least partly meant to serve Coastline, and force in that setting is not unexpectable (R2d § 228(1)(d); compare Manning and Lamkin).
Ratification is not required for respondeat superior liability.
Intentional torts can be within scope, as Manning v. Grimsley and Lamkin v. Brooks show.
A rule forbidding the conduct is a factor, not a bar (R2d § 230).
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Force on the job

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Coastline Plumbing, Inc. employs Drew as a plumber. Drew drives a Coastline van, is paid by the hour, and must follow Coastline's dispatch schedule and safety manual. Coastline's written rules forbid employees to use the van for personal errands and forbid them to argue with customers about bills; billing disputes must be sent to the office.

Assume Coastline is held liable to Elle for the lunch-run accident. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Drew remains personally liable to Elle.
Coastline may seek to recover its loss from Drew.
Elle must choose whether to sue Drew or Coastline, but may not sue both.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. An agent is always liable for his own torts, even when acting within the scope of employment (R3d § 7.01).
True. Drew breached his duty of care to Coastline, and an agent is liable to the principal for loss caused by that breach (R3d § 8.08).
False. Employer and employee are jointly and severally liable for torts within the scope of employment; Elle may sue both, though she can collect her damages only once.
Correct. Drew is liable to Elle, and Coastline may look to Drew for its loss.
C is wrong; Elle may sue both.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The employee's own liability

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Coastline Plumbing, Inc. employs Drew as a plumber. Drew drives a Coastline van, is paid by the hour, and must follow Coastline's dispatch schedule and safety manual. Coastline's written rules forbid employees to use the van for personal errands and forbid them to argue with customers about bills; billing disputes must be sent to the office.

Before hiring Drew, Coastline never checked his driving record, which shows three recent convictions for drunk driving. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Coastline cannot be liable, because Drew's convictions involved driving off duty.
Negligent hiring is a form of vicarious liability, so it applies only to acts within the scope of employment.
Coastline may be directly liable for negligent selection, even if the accident was outside the scope.
Elle must prove that Coastline intended her harm.
None of the above.
oe: Off-duty conduct is exactly what shows his unfitness for a driving job.
Negligent hiring is direct liability for the employer's own fault.
Correct. A principal is directly liable for its own negligence in selecting, training, retaining, or supervising an agent (R3d § 7.05). That liability does not depend on scope.
Direct liability under § 7.05 rests on negligence, not intent.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Negligent hiring

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nadia puts up $80,000 to open Saffron Table, a restaurant. Omar, an experienced chef, contributes no money and runs the kitchen and daily operations. They sign a document titled "Partnership Agreement" that provides: profits are split 70% to Nadia and 30% to Omar; Omar receives a fixed $1,500 per week whether or not there are profits; "Omar shall not be liable for any debts of the business"; and Nadia has final authority on all decisions. The lease, bank accounts, and liquor license are in Nadia's name alone.

Is Omar a partner of Nadia's in Saffron Table?
o: Yes, because sharing profits conclusively makes a person a partner.
Probably not; he looks like a well-paid employee despite the label and profit share.
No, because a person who contributes no capital at all cannot be a partner in the business.
Yes, because they signed a "Partnership Agreement."
None of the above.
oe: Profit sharing raises only a presumption, and the presumption does not arise when the share is received as wages.

Correct. A partnership label does not make a partnership. Weighing the factors (profit and loss sharing, control, ownership, conduct toward others), Omar looks like a well-paid employee; profit shares received as wages do not raise the § 202(c)(3) presumption (Fenwick).
No rule requires capital, much less equal capital; services alone can be a partner's contribution.
Labels don't control; what counts is whether they carry on as co-owners (§ 202(a); Fenwick).
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Label vs. substance (Fenwick)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nadia puts up $80,000 to open Saffron Table, a restaurant. Omar, an experienced chef, contributes no money and runs the kitchen and daily operations. They sign a document titled "Partnership Agreement" that provides: profits are split 70% to Nadia and 30% to Omar; Omar receives a fixed $1,500 per week whether or not there are profits; "Omar shall not be liable for any debts of the business"; and Nadia has final authority on all decisions. The lease, bank accounts, and liquor license are in Nadia's name alone.

A supplier, Pantry Co., is about to extend credit to the restaurant. Omar tells Pantry's sales rep, "Nadia and I are partners here," and Pantry relies on that statement in extending credit. Is Omar liable to Pantry for the restaurant's unpaid bill?
o: He may be, because he held himself out as a partner and Pantry relied on it.
No, because only Nadia's statements could create liability.
No, because Omar is not actually a partner.
No, because the agreement says Omar is not liable for any debts of the business.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A person who purports to be a partner is liable as one to a person who, relying on the representation, enters into a transaction with the actual or purported partnership (RUPA § 308(a); UPA § 16).
Omar's own representation is what makes him liable to a relying creditor.
Partnership by estoppel exists precisely to make a non-partner liable for his own representations.
That is a term between Nadia and Omar. It does not bind Pantry, which never agreed to it.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Purported partner (§ 308)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nadia puts up $80,000 to open Saffron Table, a restaurant. Omar, an experienced chef, contributes no money and runs the kitchen and daily operations. They sign a document titled "Partnership Agreement" that provides: profits are split 70% to Nadia and 30% to Omar; Omar receives a fixed $1,500 per week whether or not there are profits; "Omar shall not be liable for any debts of the business"; and Nadia has final authority on all decisions. The lease, bank accounts, and liquor license are in Nadia's name alone.

Now assume Omar really is a partner: he takes no weekly pay, profits are split 50/50, and losses were never discussed. The restaurant closes after losing $60,000 of Nadia's $80,000; there are no outside creditors. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Under the RUPA's default rules, Omar must contribute $30,000.
Under Kovacik v. Reed, Omar owes nothing.
Under the RUPA, Omar owes nothing, because he contributed no capital.
A and B.
B and C.
oe: True. Losses are shared in proportion to profit shares (§ 401(a)), and the RUPA's comment says this applies even when a partner contributed no capital. Each partner bears $30,000; Nadia gets the $20,000 left plus $30,000 from Omar.
True. Kovacik held that when one partner contributes only money and the other only services, each loses his own contribution: one his money, the other his labor.
False. The RUPA's comment to § 401 rejects Kovacik and applies the default loss rule anyway.
Correct. The statute and Kovacik reach opposite results on these facts.
C misstates the RUPA, which rejects the Kovacik rule.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — RUPA vs. Kovacik

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nadia puts up $80,000 to open Saffron Table, a restaurant. Omar, an experienced chef, contributes no money and runs the kitchen and daily operations. They sign a document titled "Partnership Agreement" that provides: profits are split 70% to Nadia and 30% to Omar; Omar receives a fixed $1,500 per week whether or not there are profits; "Omar shall not be liable for any debts of the business"; and Nadia has final authority on all decisions. The lease, bank accounts, and liquor license are in Nadia's name alone.

In a jurisdiction that follows Kovacik v. Reed, in which of the following situations would a court probably NOT apply the Kovacik rule to protect Omar from sharing capital losses?
o: Omar drew a $1,500 weekly salary for his work.
Omar contributed $2,000 of his own money along with his services.
Omar contributed only his services and was never paid.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Courts don't apply Kovacik when the service partner was paid for his services, because he did not lose the value of his labor.
True. Any capital contribution, even a nominal one, takes the case outside Kovacik.
False. That is the Kovacik fact pattern itself, where the rule does apply.
Correct. A salary or any capital contribution by the service partner defeats the Kovacik exception.
C is the classic case for applying Kovacik, not an exception to it.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — When Kovacik does not apply

q: Which of the following, standing alone, is NOT enough to give an agent apparent authority?
o: The principal's silence, when a reasonable person would object, while the agent claims authority in the principal's presence.
The principal's placing the agent in a position whose holders customarily have such authority.
The agent's own statement to the third party that he is authorized.
The principal's past payment of similar contracts the agent made with the same third party.
The principal's letter to the third party naming the agent as its representative.
oe: Silence where one would speak can be a manifestation (compare Ackerman, where the clients stood by during the settlement talks).
Position is a manifestation by the principal (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b; Kidd).
Correct: this is not enough. Apparent authority must be traceable to the principal's manifestations to the third party; the agent's own say-so never suffices by itself (R3d § 3.03; Lind; Hoddeson).
A prior course of dealing that the principal accepted is a manifestation to the third party.
A direct written manifestation from the principal.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Source of apparent authority

q: When a RUPA partnership is wound up, how are its assets applied?
o: First to outside creditors, then to loans from partners, then to partners' capital, and last to profits.
All creditors, including partners, then unreturned contributions, then surplus by distribution shares.
First to the partners' profits, then to their capital, and only then to the partnership's creditors.
To creditors only; partners never have to contribute if the assets fall short.
None of the above.
oe: That is the UPA (1914) § 40(b) order. RUPA no longer subordinates partner loans to outside creditors.
Correct. RUPA § 806 pays all creditors together, including partner-creditors, then returns unreturned contributions, then pays any surplus by distribution shares.
Creditors always come first.
Partners must contribute to cover shortfalls in proportion to their loss shares (except for obligations incurred while the firm was an LLP).
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — RUPA § 806 distribution

q: Under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 396, a sales agent who quits and has no non-compete agreement may:
o: Compete with her former principal.
Use the names of customers she remembers.
Use a copy of the principal's confidential customer list that she made before leaving.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. After termination, an agent is free to compete.
True under R2d § 396 (though R3d § 8.05, Illus. 7, treats using a memorized confidential list as a breach).
False. A former agent may not use written lists, trade secrets, or other confidential information (Town & Country).
Correct under R2d § 396: free competition and remembered customer names, but not confidential lists.
C is wrong; copying a confidential list before leaving is a breach.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — After the agency ends (R2d § 396)

q: Which of the following best explains why the lenders in Martin v. Peyton were not partners, while Cargill became the principal of the grain elevator it financed?
o: The Martin lenders could only veto deals, while Cargill ran Warren's business day to day.
The Martin lenders had no right to information about the firm.
Cargill shared in Warren's profits, while the Martin lenders received no share of profits.
Cargill signed an agreement calling itself Warren's principal.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Martin treated each protective term as reasonable security for a large, risky loan; vetoes are not management. Cargill crossed into control: it approved major decisions, supplied forms, and gave Warren "paternal guidance" daily.
They had broad inspection rights, which the court treated as ordinary lender protection.
Backwards in part: the Martin lenders received 40% of profits (capped), which did not make them partners.
Cargill signed no such agreement; agency arose from its conduct.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Martin v. Peyton vs. Cargill

q: In a limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), which of the following statements is true?
o: Only the limited partners are shielded; general partners remain personally liable.
It can be formed without any filing with the state.
General partners are shielded from personal liability, as well as limited partners.
It need not have a general partner.
None of the above.
oe: That describes an ordinary LP, not an LLLP.
An LLLP is an LP that elects that status in its filed certificate.
Correct. An LLLP is a limited partnership that elects LLLP status, and it treats its general partners like limited partners for liability purposes (ULPA §§ 102(10), 404(c)).
It is still a limited partnership, with general partners who manage it.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LLLPs

q: Under the RUPA, when a partner dissociates and the partnership continues, the dissociation ends which of the following?
o: The partner's right to participate in managing the business.
The partner's duty not to compete with the partnership.
The partner's liability for partnership obligations incurred while she was a partner.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. § 603(b): management rights end on dissociation (except for any role in winding up).
True. The duty not to compete ends at dissociation; the other loyalty duties continue only as to matters that arose before it.
False. Dissociation does not discharge liability for obligations incurred while a partner (§§ 603(c), 703(a)).
Correct. Management rights and the duty not to compete end; liability for past obligations does not.
C is wrong; a dissociated partner stays liable for old debts.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Effect of dissociation (§ 603)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Alison, Bill, and Carla are equal partners in Northside Grocery, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Alison handles purchasing. Carla's son, Don, works as the store's stock clerk. Fresh Farms has supplied the store's produce every week for years.

Alison and Bill vote to fire Don for repeated lateness. Carla objects. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Only a court may decide a dispute among partners about personnel.
Firing a clerk is an ordinary matter, so Alison and Bill may decide it.
Carla may veto the firing, because each partner has equal management rights.
Firing Don requires unanimous consent, because he is a partner's family member.
None of the above.
oe: Partners resolve ordinary disputes by majority vote.
Correct. Matters in the ordinary course are decided by a majority of the partners (RUPA § 401(k)). Carla's equal management right gives her a vote, not a veto. This is the casebook's grocery problem.
Equal rights mean an equal vote; a majority still decides ordinary matters.
Nothing in the statute treats family employees differently.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Ordinary matters by majority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Alison, Bill, and Carla are equal partners in Northside Grocery, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Alison handles purchasing. Carla's son, Don, works as the store's stock clerk. Fresh Farms has supplied the store's produce every week for years.

Over Carla's objection, Alison and Bill decide to sell the store building and turn Northside into an online-only delivery business. Which of the following statements is true?
o: They need Carla's consent, because the change is outside the ordinary course.
Alison alone may decide, because she handles purchasing and the store's dealings with outsiders.
They may proceed, because a majority decides all partnership matters.
Carla is dissociated by her objection.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Acts outside the ordinary course of business, and amendments to the partnership agreement, require the consent of all partners (§ 401(k)).
Her job does not give her power over fundamental changes.
A majority decides only ordinary-course matters.
Disagreement is not a dissociation event.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Outside the ordinary course

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Alison, Bill, and Carla are equal partners in Northside Grocery, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Alison handles purchasing. Carla's son, Don, works as the store's stock clerk. Fresh Farms has supplied the store's produce every week for years.

Carla tells Fresh Farms, "I won't be responsible for any more orders from you." Bill says nothing. Alison then places the usual weekly produce order. Is the partnership bound to pay for it?
o: Yes, but Carla is not personally liable, because she disclaimed responsibility.
No, because any partner may withdraw the partnership's consent to a supplier.
Yes, because Carla alone cannot restrict Alison's authority over ordinary purchases.
No, because Fresh Farms had notice that one of the partners objected to further orders.
None of the above.
oe: If the partnership is bound, every partner is personally liable for the obligation (§ 306(a)).
Not when that partner is in the minority on an ordinary-course matter.

Correct. Buying produce is ordinary business, and a single partner out of three cannot take away a co-partner's authority on ordinary matters. National Biscuit v. Stroud makes the same point: a partner who is not a majority cannot restrict a co-partner's authority over ordinary matters.
Notice matters only if Alison actually lacked authority, and one partner's objection did not take it away.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — One partner's notice to a supplier

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Alison, Bill, and Carla are equal partners in Northside Grocery, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Alison handles purchasing. Carla's son, Don, works as the store's stock clerk. Fresh Farms has supplied the store's produce every week for years.

Now assume that Bill and Carla together notify Fresh Farms in writing that the partnership will not pay for further orders. Alison orders anyway. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership is bound unless Alison agrees to the restriction.
The partnership is bound, because Alison is the purchasing partner.
The partnership is bound, because an ordinary-course purchase always binds the partnership.
No, because a majority restricted Alison's authority and Fresh Farms knew it.
None of the above.
oe: The majority does not need the restricted partner's agreement.
Her role cannot overcome a majority decision that Fresh Farms knew about.
It binds unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice. Both conditions are met here.

Correct. Under § 301, an ordinary-course act binds the partnership unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice of that. A majority of the partners took away Alison's authority, and Fresh Farms was told.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Majority restricts authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Alison, Bill, and Carla are equal partners in Northside Grocery, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Alison handles purchasing. Carla's son, Don, works as the store's stock clerk. Fresh Farms has supplied the store's produce every week for years.

Without telling Bill or Carla, Alison sells the store's surplus refrigeration unit, below market price, to a catering business she owns. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Alison committed no breach, because she handles purchasing.
Alison breached her duty of loyalty by dealing with the partnership as an adverse party.
Alison breached only her duty of care, by selling the unit without getting a fair price.
Alison committed no breach, because a partner may further her own interest.
None of the above.
oe: Her role gives her more chances to self-deal, not permission.

Correct. A partner must refrain from dealing with the partnership as, or for, an adverse party (§ 409(b)(2)); her partners may authorize the deal after full disclosure (§ 409(f)), and fairness is a defense (§ 409(g)). A below-market sale made in secret will be hard to defend.
This is a loyalty problem: she was on both sides of the sale.
§ 409(e) says that furthering one's own interest is not by itself a breach; it does not permit secret self-dealing.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Selling to oneself

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tomas is the purchasing director of Ridgeview Hospital. Without telling the hospital, he owns 40% of MedSupply, Inc., which has won several hospital supply contracts that Tomas helped award. The prices were competitive and the hospital lost no money on them. Tomas also has the hospital's lab send overflow test orders, which he decides the lab cannot handle in time, to a private lab he owns, which charges the patients' insurers a markup.

Ridgeview discovers Tomas's interest in MedSupply. Tomas argues that he committed no breach because MedSupply's prices were competitive and the hospital lost no money. Which case best supports the hospital?
o: Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch.
Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery.
Gorton v. Doty.
Rose v. Giamatti.
Rash v. J.V. Intermediate, Ltd.
oe: Corroon & Black is about a departing agent soliciting customers whose lists were not trade secrets.
Town & Country is about ex-employees using a confidential customer list after leaving.
Gorton is about whether a gratuitous favor created an agency at all.
Rose is about whether the Commissioner was MLB's agent for discipline.

Correct. In Rash, a division manager secretly owned the scaffolding company that won subcontracts he helped award. His failure to disclose was a breach of fiduciary duty as a matter of law; an agent may not contract with his principal through his own company without its full knowledge.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Undisclosed self-dealing (Rash)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tomas is the purchasing director of Ridgeview Hospital. Without telling the hospital, he owns 40% of MedSupply, Inc., which has won several hospital supply contracts that Tomas helped award. The prices were competitive and the hospital lost no money on them. Tomas also has the hospital's lab send overflow test orders, which he decides the lab cannot handle in time, to a private lab he owns, which charges the patients' insurers a markup.

Which of the following is the hospital's best response to Tomas's argument that it suffered no loss?
o: An agent must disgorge profits made through his position whether or not the principal lost anything.
The hospital may recover only nominal damages.
Tomas's ownership share was too small to create a conflict.
The hospital must first prove that it could have bought the same supplies more cheaply from someone else.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Reading v. Regem: the army sergeant had to give up money he made by using his uniform and position even though the Crown lost nothing. Disgorgement removes the incentive to breach.
It can recover Tomas's profits, which may be far more than nominal.
A 40% stake in a company he steered contracts to is a serious conflict.
Loss is not an element of a disgorgement claim for breach of loyalty.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — No loss required

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tomas is the purchasing director of Ridgeview Hospital. Without telling the hospital, he owns 40% of MedSupply, Inc., which has won several hospital supply contracts that Tomas helped award. The prices were competitive and the hospital lost no money on them. Tomas also has the hospital's lab send overflow test orders, which he decides the lab cannot handle in time, to a private lab he owns, which charges the patients' insurers a markup.

Tomas argues that the overflow lab orders were orders the hospital lab could not handle, so the hospital lost nothing when he sent them to his own lab. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Tomas committed no breach, because the patients' insurers, not the hospital, paid his lab.
Tomas breached only his duty of obedience.
Tomas had to disclose the orders and let the hospital decide what to do with them.
Tomas committed no breach, because the hospital lab could not have done the work in time.
None of the above.
oe: The question is whether he profited from his position without disclosure, not who paid.
Secretly profiting from orders that came to him through his job is a loyalty breach.

Correct. General Automotive v. Singer: the manager who sent orders he thought the shop could not fill to other shops and kept the markup had to give up those profits. An agent cannot decide for himself which opportunities belong to the principal.
That is the argument Singer lost. The principal, not the agent, decides whether it wants the business.
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Deciding for the principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tomas is the purchasing director of Ridgeview Hospital. Without telling the hospital, he owns 40% of MedSupply, Inc., which has won several hospital supply contracts that Tomas helped award. The prices were competitive and the hospital lost no money on them. Tomas also has the hospital's lab send overflow test orders, which he decides the lab cannot handle in time, to a private lab he owns, which charges the patients' insurers a markup.

Suppose Tomas had asked the hospital's board in advance for permission to keep his MedSupply stake. Under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 8.06, which of the following would the board's consent require?
o: Tomas acts in good faith.
Tomas discloses all material facts that he knows or should know would affect the board's judgment.
Tomas otherwise deals fairly with the hospital, and the consent covers a specific act or type of act.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Consent is effective only if the agent acts in good faith.
True. Full disclosure is required.
True. The agent must deal fairly, and a general blanket waiver will not do.
Incomplete. Fair dealing and a specific scope are also required.
Correct. § 8.06 requires good faith, disclosure of all material facts, fair dealing, and consent to a specific act or type of act.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Effective consent (§ 8.06)

q: Which of the following facts would most strongly support a finding that a lender had become the principal of the business it financed?
o: The lender holds a security interest in the borrower's equipment.
The lender decides which contracts the borrower makes and runs its daily operations.
The lender may veto the borrower's speculative investments.
The lender requires the borrower to send it monthly financial statements and annual audits.
The lender charges a high interest rate because the borrower is risky.
oe: Taking collateral is what lenders do; it shows no control of the business.
Correct. Cargill: a creditor that takes over management of its debtor becomes a principal (R2d § 14O). Directing contracts and daily operations is control, not mere protection of a loan.
A veto over risky deals is protective (Martin v. Peyton); the power to initiate and direct is what matters.
Information rights are ordinary lender protection (Martin v. Peyton).
Pricing for risk has nothing to do with control.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Creditor control (Cargill)

q: Curt orders $40,000 of lumber, signing "Coastal Builders Exchange, by Curt, Officer." No company by that name exists; Curt actually works for Delmar Construction, Inc., whose name the seller could have found in public records. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Curt is personally liable on the contract, because he did not disclose his principal's identity.
Only Delmar is liable, once it is identified.
Curt is not liable, because the seller could easily have identified Delmar by searching the public records.
Curt is not liable, because he signed as an officer rather than in his own name.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. An agent for an unidentified (partially disclosed) principal is a party to the contract (R3d § 6.02). The burden is on the agent to disclose; the seller's ability to search records does not matter (Atlantic Salmon v. Curran).
Delmar may be liable once identified, but Curt is liable alongside it.
Atlantic Salmon rejected this argument; the agent must disclose.
Signing as "officer" of a nonexistent company does not disclose the real principal.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Unidentified principal

q: Lars's personal creditor, not a creditor of the partnership, wins a judgment against him and obtains a charging order against his transferable interest in a RUPA partnership. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The creditor becomes a partner in Lars's place.
Lars is automatically dissociated.
The creditor gets Lars's distributions, but no role in management.
The creditor may seize partnership equipment to satisfy the judgment.
None of the above.
oe: At most, the creditor (or a buyer at foreclosure) becomes a transferee, not a partner.
A charging order is not a dissociation event.

Correct. A charging order is a lien on the judgment debtor's transferable interest that requires the partnership to pay the creditor any distribution owed to the debtor (§ 504). It gives no management or information rights.
Partnership property belongs to the entity, not to Lars, and his personal creditors cannot reach it directly.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Charging order

q: In Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim, the court allowed Kim's claims against his former business partner to go forward because:
o: An oral partnership agreement for a technology business must be in writing to be enforced.
Incorporating the business ended all partnership duties.
Kim had a non-compete agreement with his partner.
A partner may not dissolve the firm to take the business without compensating his partner.
None of the above.
oe: A partnership needs no writing; Kim alleged an oral agreement to be equal partners.
Incorporating did not erase the duties owed while the partnership was being wound up.
The case turns on partnership fiduciary duties, not a non-compete.
Correct. The court applied Page v. Page's anti-freeze-out principle: Babineau could not lock Kim out, incorporate the business, and keep it for himself without accounting to Kim.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Second Measure v. Kim

q: Under the ULLCA, in a manager-managed LLC, which of the following statements is true?
o: The managers must be chosen by a unanimous vote of the members.
The managers owe the duties of loyalty and care; members owe none just by being members.
A manager may amend the operating agreement without the members' consent.
Every member owes the LLC the same duties of loyalty and care as the managers.
None of the above.
oe: By default a manager is chosen, and may be removed, by a majority of the members.
Correct. In a manager-managed LLC, the § 409 duties fall on the managers; members owe no fiduciary duties merely as members (§ 409(g)).
Amending the operating agreement requires the consent of all members (§ 407).
That is the rule for member-managed LLCs.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Manager-managed LLC duties

q: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of a general partnership compared with an LLC?
o: Unlimited personal liability of the owners.
Problems with expansion, succession, and termination.
The risk that the firm can be formed by accident.
Each owner's power to bind the business as its agent.
A single layer of income tax.
oe: A disadvantage. Partners are personally liable (§ 306(a)); LLC members are not (§ 304).
A disadvantage listed on the entity-selection slide.
A disadvantage: two people carrying on a business as co-owners form a partnership whether or not they intend to (§ 202(a)).
A disadvantage: every partner is an agent of the partnership (§ 301), while an LLC member is not an agent solely by being a member (ULLCA § 301).
Correct: this is not a disadvantage. Pass-through taxation is an advantage of general partnerships, and LLCs share it.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Not a disadvantage

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Lou, Mara, and Ned are partners in Lakeside Press, a print shop. They have no agreed term. Mara contributed $90,000 in capital, and Lou and Ned contributed $30,000 each. They agreed to share profits equally and said nothing about losses or about what happens when a partner leaves. In Year 4, Ned gives notice that he is leaving the partnership.

What is the effect of Ned's notice under the UPA (1914)?
o: The partnership is dissolved, rightfully, and enters winding up.
The partnership continues automatically, and Lou and Mara must buy Ned's interest within 120 days.
Ned's departure is wrongful, because he gave no advance notice.
The partnership terminates at once and must stop all business immediately.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the UPA, any partner's departure dissolves the partnership (§§ 29, 31). In an at-will partnership a partner has both the power and the right to dissolve, and dissolution starts winding up rather than ending the partnership (§ 30).
That resembles the RUPA Article 7 buyout. The UPA has no dissociation-without-dissolution path.
No term or notice requirement was agreed, so leaving an at-will partnership is rightful.
Dissolution is not termination; the partnership continues to wind up its affairs.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — At-will departure under the UPA

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Lou, Mara, and Ned are partners in Lakeside Press, a print shop. They have no agreed term. Mara contributed $90,000 in capital, and Lou and Ned contributed $30,000 each. They agreed to share profits equally and said nothing about losses or about what happens when a partner leaves. In Year 4, Ned gives notice that he is leaving the partnership.

Lou and Mara want to keep the shop running. Ned insists that all of the assets be sold. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Under UPA § 38(1), after a rightful dissolution Ned may have the partnership property applied to its debts and the surplus paid in cash.
Some courts let the continuing partners buy out the departing partner instead of selling the business, but only at a fair market value proven by evidence.
Lou and Mara may continue the business by paying Ned the book value of his interest, without goodwill.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. That is the traditional right to force a liquidation.
True. Disotell v. Stiltner held that § 38(1) does not absolutely require liquidation, but the buyout must be at proven fair market value.
False. Paying a partner's interest without goodwill is the § 38(2) remedy against a wrongful dissolver, and Ned left rightfully.
Correct. Ned has the traditional right to a liquidation, though some courts allow a buyout at proven fair market value instead.
C is wrong; Ned did not dissolve wrongfully.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Forced liquidation and its limits

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Lou, Mara, and Ned are partners in Lakeside Press, a print shop. They have no agreed term. Mara contributed $90,000 in capital, and Lou and Ned contributed $30,000 each. They agreed to share profits equally and said nothing about losses or about what happens when a partner leaves. In Year 4, Ned gives notice that he is leaving the partnership.

The assets are sold for $120,000. The partnership owes outside creditors $30,000 and owes Mara $20,000 on a loan she made to the firm. Under UPA § 40(b), how are the proceeds applied?
o: $40,000 to each partner, because the partners share equally.
$120,000 toward the return of capital first, with creditors paid out of any profits.
$30,000 to outside creditors, $20,000 to Mara's loan, then $70,000 toward capital.
$20,000 to Mara on her loan first, because partners' claims come before outsiders'.
None of the above.
oe: Equal sharing applies to profits and losses, not to the order of payment.
Capital comes after all liabilities, including partners' loans.
Correct. § 40(b) pays (I) outside creditors, (II) partners for liabilities other than capital and profits (Mara's loan), (III) capital, and (IV) profits. That leaves $70,000 for capital.
Outside creditors come first under § 40(b).
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — UPA § 40(b) in order

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Lou, Mara, and Ned are partners in Lakeside Press, a print shop. They have no agreed term. Mara contributed $90,000 in capital, and Lou and Ned contributed $30,000 each. They agreed to share profits equally and said nothing about losses or about what happens when a partner leaves. In Year 4, Ned gives notice that he is leaving the partnership.

Continuing from the prior question, $70,000 is left to repay $150,000 of capital. Under the UPA's default rules, how much will Mara receive in return of her capital?
o: None of the above.
oe: Wrong. That is not the result of any of the loss-sharing rules; see E.
That splits the $70,000 in proportion to capital contributed (90/150), a rule the slides list as one possibility, but not the statutory default.
That treats Mara's capital as senior to Lou's and Ned's; capital claims are equal in rank.
There is not enough money to repay her in full, and she must bear her share of the loss.

Correct. The $80,000 capital loss is shared like profits, equally (§ 18(a)), so each partner bears about $26,667. Mara gets $90,000 − $26,667 = $63,333, and Lou and Ned get $3,333 each, which uses the $70,000. That figure is not among A–D.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Sharing the capital loss

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Lou, Mara, and Ned are partners in Lakeside Press, a print shop. They have no agreed term. Mara contributed $90,000 in capital, and Lou and Ned contributed $30,000 each. They agreed to share profits equally and said nothing about losses or about what happens when a partner leaves. In Year 4, Ned gives notice that he is leaving the partnership.

During the winding up, Lou signs a new three-year lease for a second shop with Lessor, who had extended credit to Lakeside before the dissolution and has no knowledge or notice of it. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership is bound, and Lou is not answerable to his partners, because the lease was valid.
The partnership is not bound, because a partner has no power to bind the firm after dissolution.
The partnership is bound to Lessor, but Lou had no actual authority and is answerable to his partners.
The partnership is bound only because a new lease is an act appropriate for winding up.
None of the above.
oe: Binding the firm to new business without authority is a wrong against the other partners.
A partner keeps the power to bind for acts appropriate to winding up and, as to creditors without notice, for other acts too.

Correct. Dissolution ends actual authority except to wind up (UPA § 33), but under § 35 a partner still binds the firm by acts toward someone who extended credit before dissolution and had no knowledge or notice of it.
A new three-year lease for a second shop is new business, not winding up.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Winding-up authority (UPA § 35)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harbor Credit Union's bylaws provide that only its board of directors may settle loan-collection lawsuits. Mira, the collections manager, agrees with a borrower, Otis, to settle a $50,000 claim for $30,000. Her settlement letter, on Harbor letterhead, states: "This settlement binds Harbor Credit Union and releases all claims." Otis sends a $30,000 check with the signed letter. Harbor's treasurer deposits the check, and the board, told about the settlement at its next meeting, says nothing for six months before trying to sue Otis for the remaining $20,000.

Which theory most strongly supports Otis's argument that Harbor is bound by the settlement?
o: Inherent agency power, because the Restatement (Third) adopts it.
Ratification, because Harbor knowingly kept the $30,000 payment and stayed silent for six months.
Implied actual authority, because settling lawsuits is incidental to running a collections department.
Express actual authority, because Mira is the collections manager.
None of the above.
oe: The R3d abandons inherent agency power.

Correct. Accepting the benefits with knowledge of the material facts, and silence where one would be expected to object, are ratifying conduct (Trustees v. Steven Scott: the fund that cashed the employer's checks was bound).
An agent cannot reasonably believe she has authority that the principal's rules expressly withhold.
The bylaws reserve settlement to the board, so Mira had no express authority.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification by keeping the money

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harbor Credit Union's bylaws provide that only its board of directors may settle loan-collection lawsuits. Mira, the collections manager, agrees with a borrower, Otis, to settle a $50,000 claim for $30,000. Her settlement letter, on Harbor letterhead, states: "This settlement binds Harbor Credit Union and releases all claims." Otis sends a $30,000 check with the signed letter. Harbor's treasurer deposits the check, and the board, told about the settlement at its next meeting, says nothing for six months before trying to sue Otis for the remaining $20,000.

Harbor's board argues that it accepted the $30,000 but never agreed to release the rest of the claim. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Harbor cannot keep the payment and reject the release; it ratified the whole settlement.
Ratification requires a written board resolution.
Harbor may keep the $30,000 it received and sue Otis for the remaining $20,000 of the claim.
Harbor may undo its ratification at any time, because Mira lacked authority.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Ratification of part of a transaction ratifies all of it (R3d § 4.07). Harbor must take the settlement as a whole or give back the money and reject it, if it still can.
Ratification may be implied from conduct.
That is an attempted partial ratification, which the law does not allow.
Ratification relates back and gives the act the effect of actual authority; it cannot be withdrawn at will.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — No partial ratification

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harbor Credit Union's bylaws provide that only its board of directors may settle loan-collection lawsuits. Mira, the collections manager, agrees with a borrower, Otis, to settle a $50,000 claim for $30,000. Her settlement letter, on Harbor letterhead, states: "This settlement binds Harbor Credit Union and releases all claims." Otis sends a $30,000 check with the signed letter. Harbor's treasurer deposits the check, and the board, told about the settlement at its next meeting, says nothing for six months before trying to sue Otis for the remaining $20,000.

Now assume that, before signing, Otis's lawyer received a copy of Harbor's bylaws showing that only the board may settle lawsuits. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Mira still had apparent authority, because her letter was on Harbor letterhead and said it bound Harbor.
Harbor cannot ratify, because Otis knew Mira lacked authority.
Otis loses, because Mira lacked actual authority.
Mira had no apparent authority as to Otis, but Harbor may still be bound by ratification.
None of the above.
