oe: Letterhead cannot overcome the third party's actual knowledge of the limit.
A principal can ratify an act it knows was unauthorized; that is the point of ratification.
Lack of actual authority is cured by ratification.

Correct. Apparent authority depends on the third party's reasonable belief; once Otis knew the real limits, his belief was not reasonable (compare Steven Scott, where apparent authority lasted only until the employer learned of the board's exclusive power). Ratification does not depend on the third party's belief.
D is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Notice of real limits

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harbor Credit Union's bylaws provide that only its board of directors may settle loan-collection lawsuits. Mira, the collections manager, agrees with a borrower, Otis, to settle a $50,000 claim for $30,000. Her settlement letter, on Harbor letterhead, states: "This settlement binds Harbor Credit Union and releases all claims." Otis sends a $30,000 check with the signed letter. Harbor's treasurer deposits the check, and the board, told about the settlement at its next meeting, says nothing for six months before trying to sue Otis for the remaining $20,000.

Assume instead that Harbor's board promptly rejected the settlement and returned the check, and that Otis did not know Mira lacked authority. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Mira cannot be liable, because she was acting for a disclosed principal.
Mira is liable to Otis for his loss on her implied warranty of authority.
Otis's only remedy is against Harbor.
Mira is liable only if she knew she lacked authority.
None of the above.
oe: An agent of a disclosed principal is not a party to an authorized contract, but she is liable on her warranty when she had no authority.

Correct. A person who purports to make a contract for a principal impliedly warrants her power to bind it, and is liable to a third party who did not know otherwise (R3d § 6.10), unless the principal ratifies or she disclaimed the warranty.
Harbor is not bound, so Otis's remedy is against Mira.
The warranty does not require knowledge or fraud.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Implied warranty of authority

q: Which of the following is NOT required to create an agency relationship?
o: An understanding that the principal will control the undertaking.
The agent's acceptance of the undertaking.
A contract supported by consideration.
The principal's manifestation that the agent will act on the principal's behalf.
None of the above; all of them are required.
oe: Required, though control can be minimal; the right to control, not its exercise, matters.
Required. The agent must manifest assent or otherwise consent to act.
Correct: this is not required. Agency rests on consent, not contract; a gratuitous agent is still an agent (Gorton v. Doty).
Required. It is the first of the three elements (R3d § 1.01; Botticello).
C is not required.

q: Which of the following facts most strongly suggests that a gas station operator is the oil company's servant (employee) rather than an independent contractor?
o: The company sets the station's hours and may end the deal or reassign him at will.
The oil company trains the operator and makes suggestions on weekly visits.
The station displays the oil company's brand and logo.
The operator buys all of his gasoline from the oil company.
The oil company owns the land under the station.
oe: Correct. Those were the facts of Humble Oil v. Martin, where the company kept the right to control the station's daily operation, so the operator was its servant despite a contract calling him independent.
In Hoover, training and weekly suggestions that the dealer could ignore were not control.
Branding alone does not show control of daily operations (Hoover v. Sun Oil).
A supply relationship is not control over the manner and means of the work.
Sun Oil owned and leased the station in Hoover too; ownership alone was not enough.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Humble Oil vs. Hoover

q: Under the Restatement (Second) of Agency § 379, which of the following statements about an agent's duty of care is true?
o: Paid and unpaid agents are always held to exactly the same standard of care.
A gratuitous agent is held to a lower standard of care than a paid agent.
A gratuitous agent owes no fiduciary duties at all.
An agent with special skill is held only to the care of an ordinary person.
None of the above.
oe: R2d § 379 distinguishes them.
Correct. The standard of care slides with skill and may vary with compensation; a gratuitous agent owes reasonable care but a lower standard. His duty of loyalty is not reduced.
An unpaid agent is still a fiduciary and owes full loyalty.
An agent with special skill must use it.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Care: paid vs. gratuitous agents

q: Vera leases a storefront to a bakery for rent equal to 8% of the bakery's net profits. Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), which of the following statements is true?
o: Vera is a partner only if she has also agreed to share losses.
Vera is a partner, because the bakery operates in a building she owns.
Vera is presumed to be a partner, because her payment varies with the bakery's profits.
Vera is presumed to be a partner, but she can rebut the presumption by showing that she never managed the bakery.
None of the above.
oe: Loss sharing is a factor, but the rent exception decides the presumption question here.
Co-ownership or ownership of property used by the business does not make a partnership.
A share received as rent is one of the listed exceptions.
Wrong. No presumption arises in the first place, because the profit share was received as rent (§ 202(c)(3)).

Correct. Profit sharing raises a presumption of partnership unless the profits were received in payment of rent, among other things (§ 202(c)(3)). Vera's share is rent, so no presumption arises, and nothing else suggests she co-owns the bakery.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Rent that varies with profits

q: Under the RUPA, a filed statement of dissociation:
o: Releases the dissociated partner from all debts incurred while he was a partner.
Is required for a dissociation to be effective at all.
Takes effect against every third party, as notice of the dissociation, on the day it is filed.
Gives outsiders notice of the dissociation 90 days after it takes effect.
None of the above.
oe: Dissociation does not discharge existing liabilities (§ 703(a)).
A partner is dissociated by the event itself (§ 601); the statement only gives notice.
Constructive notice arrives 90 days after filing; actual notice works sooner.
Correct. Persons who are not partners are deemed to have notice of the dissociation 90 days after the statement becomes effective (§§ 103(d), 704), which ends the two-year § 702 window early.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Statement of dissociation

q: Which of the following is NOT a typical purpose of a buyout agreement?
o: Making sure a departing partner is always paid the liquidation value of the business.
Passing the business to the right family members.
Creating a market for the interests of inactive owners.
Letting the remaining owners keep control of the business and choose who may become a new owner.
Providing for an orderly transfer of a departing owner's interest.
oe: Correct: this is not a purpose. Buyout agreements set a price or formula the parties choose, often to avoid liquidation and its fire-sale values.
A typical purpose.
A typical purpose. Without one, an interest in a closely held firm may be unsellable.
A typical purpose.
A typical purpose.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Purposes of a buyout agreement

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Harbor Lane Properties, LLC, formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA), owns three apartment buildings. Its members are Pia (60%), Quinn (20%), and Ravi (20%). The operating agreement makes the LLC manager-managed and names Pia as its only manager. It also provides: "The manager may engage in other real estate businesses, including businesses that compete with the Company." Quinn and Ravi have no management role.

Without consulting Quinn or Ravi, Pia signs a contract selling all three of the LLC's buildings to a buyer. Under the ULLCA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Pia may make the sale alone, because a manager decides every matter in a manager-managed LLC.
Pia may make the sale because she holds 60% of the membership interests.
Pia needed all the members' consent, because the sale is outside the ordinary course.
Quinn and Ravi have no say, because members of a manager-managed LLC have no voting rights.
None of the above.
oe: Managers decide ordinary matters; fundamental transactions still need all the members.
The statute requires all members, not a majority by interest.

Correct. Even in a manager-managed LLC, the consent of all members is required to dispose of all or substantially all of the company's property outside the ordinary course, to act outside the ordinary course, or to amend the operating agreement (§ 407).
Members keep their votes on fundamental matters and on choosing and removing managers.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Selling substantially all assets

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Harbor Lane Properties, LLC, formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA), owns three apartment buildings. Its members are Pia (60%), Quinn (20%), and Ravi (20%). The operating agreement makes the LLC manager-managed and names Pia as its only manager. It also provides: "The manager may engage in other real estate businesses, including businesses that compete with the Company." Quinn and Ravi have no management role.

Quinn signs a contract in the LLC's name hiring Topline Roofing to replace a roof. Topline assumed that any member could sign for the LLC. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Quinn is personally liable for all of the LLC's debts because he signed without authority.
Membership alone does not make Quinn an agent; Topline must rely on agency law.
The LLC is bound only if Quinn holds a majority of the membership interests.
The LLC is bound, because every member of an LLC is its agent, just as every partner is an agent of a partnership.
None of the above.
oe: At most Quinn is liable on this contract on his implied warranty of authority; he does not become liable for the LLC's other debts.
Correct. Under ULLCA § 301, a member is not an agent of the LLC solely by being a member. Whether the LLC is bound depends on ordinary agency principles or a filed statement of authority.
Ownership percentage does not create agency.
That is the partnership rule (RUPA § 301), which the ULLCA deliberately does not follow.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — A member is not an agent by status

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Harbor Lane Properties, LLC, formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA), owns three apartment buildings. Its members are Pia (60%), Quinn (20%), and Ravi (20%). The operating agreement makes the LLC manager-managed and names Pia as its only manager. It also provides: "The manager may engage in other real estate businesses, including businesses that compete with the Company." Quinn and Ravi have no management role.

Pia buys a fourth apartment building nearby for herself, and it competes with Harbor Lane for tenants. Quinn claims Pia breached her duty of loyalty. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The clause is void, because the duty of loyalty can never be changed by agreement.
Pia committed no breach because a manager owes no fiduciary duties.
Pia breached her duty, because no manager may ever compete with the LLC, whatever the agreement says.
The clause is likely enforceable, because loyalty may be narrowed if not manifestly unreasonable.
None of the above.
oe: Loyalty cannot be eliminated, but it can be restricted and tailored.
Managers of a manager-managed LLC owe the § 409 duties; the clause narrows them only as to competition.
Competing is a default breach, and the agreement can change that default.

Correct. ULLCA § 105 bars eliminating the duty of loyalty, but if not manifestly unreasonable, the agreement may narrow it and identify specific permitted activities. Pia still owes good faith and fair dealing, which cannot be eliminated.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Tailoring loyalty in the operating agreement

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Harbor Lane Properties, LLC, formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA), owns three apartment buildings. Its members are Pia (60%), Quinn (20%), and Ravi (20%). The operating agreement makes the LLC manager-managed and names Pia as its only manager. It also provides: "The manager may engage in other real estate businesses, including businesses that compete with the Company." Quinn and Ravi have no management role.

Pia has the LLC pay her a large "management bonus" that leaves it unable to pay its contractors. Quinn wants to sue Pia. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Quinn's claim is derivative, so she must first make a demand or show futility.
Quinn's only remedy is to withdraw and demand a buyout of her interest.
Quinn has no remedy, because members of a manager-managed LLC cannot sue managers.
Quinn may sue directly, because the value of her interest went down.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The injury is to the LLC, and a member's loss in value is only derivative of it. A member may sue directly only for an injury not solely the result of an injury to the company (§ 801); a derivative action requires a demand or a showing of futility (§ 802).
The ULLCA gives a withdrawing member no buyout right; she would hold her interest as a transferee.
Members can bring derivative actions for harm managers do to the company.
A drop in the value of her interest is the classic derivative injury.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Direct vs. derivative suit

Q7–11 HYPO: Harbor Lane Properties, LLC, formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA), owns three apartment buildings. Its members are Pia (60%), Quinn (20%), and Ravi (20%). The operating agreement makes the LLC manager-managed and names Pia as its only manager. Quinn applies for a court order dissolving the LLC, alleging that Pia, who controls it, has acted oppressively and in a way directly harmful to Quinn. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Oppressive conduct by those in control that directly harms the applicant is a ground for judicial dissolution.
The court may order a remedy other than dissolution.
The operating agreement could have eliminated this ground for dissolution.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. ULLCA § 701.
True. The court may order a lesser remedy (§ 701(b)), such as a buyout.
False. The operating agreement cannot vary the grounds for judicial dissolution (§ 105).
Correct. Oppression is a ground, and the court has flexibility in the remedy.
C is wrong; the judicial dissolution grounds are mandatory.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess is building a deck. As a favor, she asks her neighbor Ugo to drive her pickup truck to Lumber Barn and buy 40 boards, telling him, "Put it on my account, and take Route 9, not the highway." Ugo has run two similar errands for Tess before, and both times Lumber Barn's clerk saw Tess thank Ugo and pay the bill. Tess does not pay Ugo anything.

Which of the following best describes the relationship between Tess and Ugo for the Lumber Barn errand?
o: There is no agency, because Ugo receives no compensation.
There is no agency, because nothing was put in writing.
Ugo is Tess's agent for the errand, even though he is unpaid.
Ugo is an independent contractor who owes Tess no duties.
None of the above.
oe: Payment is not required; a gratuitous agent is still an agent.
Agency needs no writing unless a statute requires one.

Correct. Tess manifested that Ugo would act for her, Ugo consented by going, and Tess controlled the undertaking (what to buy, whose account, which route). No consideration is required (Gorton v. Doty).
He acts for her, with her consent and subject to her control, so he is her agent and fiduciary.
C is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess is building a deck. As a favor, she asks her neighbor Ugo to drive her pickup truck to Lumber Barn and buy 40 boards, telling him, "Put it on my account, and take Route 9, not the highway." Ugo has run two similar errands for Tess before, and both times Lumber Barn's clerk saw Tess thank Ugo and pay the bill. Tess does not pay Ugo anything.

On the way to Lumber Barn, Ugo runs a red light and injures Vic. Can Vic recover from Tess?
o: Yes, but only because Tess owns the truck.
Possibly, because an unpaid agent on her errand, under her control, can make her liable.
No, because only Ugo was negligent.
No, because Ugo was doing Tess a favor as a neighbor rather than working for her for pay.
None of the above.
oe: Ownership alone is not the basis; the agency relationship and Tess's control are.
Correct. In Gorton v. Doty, the teacher who lent her car on the condition that the coach drive it was liable for his negligence. Working without pay is no defense, and Tess even chose his route.
Ugo is liable for his own tort, but respondeat superior makes the principal answer too.
Gratuitous service does not defeat vicarious liability.
B is correct.

As a favor, she asks her neighbor Ugo to drive her pickup truck to Lumber Barn and buy 40 boards, telling him, "Put it on my account, and take Route 9, not the highway." Ugo also picks out a $600 power saw for himself and charges it to Tess's account. The clerk assumes that Tess approved. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ugo had no actual authority to buy the saw.
Tess may be bound if Lumber Barn reasonably believed, from Tess's past conduct, that Ugo could charge items to her account.
Ugo is liable to Tess for any loss he causes her by acting beyond his authority.
A and B.
A, B and C.

True. Tess's prior acceptance of Ugo's purchases, in front of the clerk, is a manifestation that can support apparent authority if the clerk's belief was reasonable.

Incomplete. Ugo is also liable to Tess.

Ugo has run two similar errands for Tess before, and both times Lumber Barn's clerk saw Tess thank Ugo and pay the bill. Tess does not pay Ugo anything.

Lumber Barn gives Ugo a $50 gift card "for bringing in Tess's business." Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ugo may keep the gift card, because he is not paid for his services.
Ugo may keep the gift card, because Tess lost nothing.
Ugo must account to Tess for the gift card, because even an unpaid agent owes a duty of loyalty.
Ugo must account for the gift card only if Tess told him in advance not to accept gifts.
None of the above.
oe: Loyalty does not depend on compensation.
Loss to the principal is irrelevant to the duty to account (Reading v. Regem).
Correct. An agent may not acquire a material benefit from a third party in connection with the agency (R3d § 8.02). Being unpaid lowers the standard of care, not the duty of loyalty.
The duty arises from the agency itself, not from an instruction.
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Loyalty of an unpaid agent

q: Under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 2.06(1), an undisclosed principal is liable to a third party who justifiably changes position in reliance on an agent's unauthorized conduct if:
o: The principal, on notice of the agent's conduct, did not take reasonable steps to notify others.
The principal later ratified the conduct after learning all the facts.
The third party knew the principal's identity when the contract was made.
The agent signed the contract in the principal's name rather than in his own name.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2.06(1) is an estoppel-like rule that replaces part of the old inherent-agency doctrine: the undisclosed principal pays when it stood by after learning what its agent was doing.
Ratification is a separate basis for liability; § 2.06(1) applies without it.
If the third party knew the principal, it would not be undisclosed.
An undisclosed principal is, by definition, not named.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — R3d § 2.06(1)

q: In deciding whether a general partnership exists, which of the following is LEAST relevant?
o: Whether the parties share losses.
Whether each party has a right to take part in management.
How the parties reported the business on their tax returns.
Whether the parties contributed capital.
Whether the parties filed a certificate with the state.
oe: Relevant: loss sharing shows risk, a key partnership factor (Kaufman-Brown).
Relevant: control is a core factor.
Relevant: it shows how the parties dealt with third parties and how they saw their relationship.
Relevant (Zajac v. Harris).
Correct. A general partnership needs no filing, so the absence of one says nothing about whether it exists.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Least relevant factor

q: Under the ULLCA, a judgment creditor of the only member of a single-member LLC:
o: Becomes the LLC's manager.
May seize the LLC's property directly.
May foreclose on its charging order, and the buyer gets the member's entire interest.
Can only collect distributions, because a charging order is always the exclusive remedy.
None of the above.
oe: A creditor's remedies are economic; no management role comes with them.
The LLC is a separate entity; its assets are not the member's.
Correct. A charging order is usually the exclusive remedy, but when the debtor is the sole member, foreclosure passes the member's entire interest, not just the right to distributions (§ 503).
That is the rule for multi-member LLCs, not single-member ones.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Charging order on a sole member

q: In a RUPA partnership, partner Lee personally pays a $10,000 partnership debt incurred in the ordinary course, and he also advances $20,000 to the partnership beyond his agreed capital contribution. Absent a contrary agreement, which of the following statements is true?
o: Neither payment is recoverable, because a partner has no right to compensation.
The $10,000 must be reimbursed, and the $20,000 is a loan that accrues interest.
Lee may recover the $10,000 only from his co-partners personally, not from the partnership.
Both payments are additional capital contributions, repayable only on liquidation.
None of the above.
oe: The no-compensation rule concerns pay for services, not reimbursement or loans.

Correct. The partnership must reimburse a partner for payments made in the ordinary course (§ 401(c)), and an advance beyond the agreed contribution is a loan to the partnership that accrues interest (§ 401(d)–(e)).
The partnership itself owes the reimbursement.
Payments in the ordinary course and advances beyond agreed capital are treated as loans or indemnifiable payments, not capital.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Indemnity and advances

q: An agent's duty to give the principal information (R3d § 8.11) does NOT require disclosure when:
o: The agent owes a superior duty to another person not to reveal the information.
Disclosure would embarrass the agent.
The information is bad news for the principal.
The agent believes the principal would not care, even though the fact is material.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 8.11 requires reasonable effort to provide facts the principal would want or that are material, unless doing so would violate a superior duty the agent owes to another person, such as a confidentiality duty to another client.
The agent's embarrassment is no excuse.
Bad news is often exactly what the principal most needs.
If the fact is material, the agent must disclose it whatever he guesses about the principal's interest.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Limit on the duty to disclose

q: Which of the following best reflects the course's critique of Kovacik v. Reed?
o: The capital partner should always bear every loss, because he had more to lose.
Kovacik is plainly right, because a partner's services, unlike money, cannot lose value in a failed venture.
A real bargain would likely fall between equal sharing and zero loss for the service partner.
The RUPA codified the Kovacik rule.
None of the above.
oe: That is the Kovacik result itself, which the critique questions.
The service partner's labor is exactly what Kovacik treats as lost.

Correct. The hypothetical-bargain model suggests a middle ground without saying where it lies. Since losses often trace to the service partner's work, and Kovacik may encourage his risk-taking, the capital partner would likely insist on some loss sharing.
The comment to RUPA § 401 rejects Kovacik.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — The professor's critique of Kovacik

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina each put $100,000 into a joint bank account and use it to buy Mill Creek, a 20-acre parcel, planning to resell it within two years and split the profit equally. They take title in the name "Mill Creek Ventures." They have no written agreement. Cole, who handles zoning, learns from the county planner that the adjoining 10 acres will soon be offered for sale and that combining the two tracts would double Mill Creek's value.

What is the most accurate description of the relationship among Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina?
o: They owe one another no duties, because a single deal cannot be a partnership.
Probably joint venturers, governed by partnership law, including the duty of loyalty.
They are merely tenants in common of the land.
They cannot be joint venturers without a written agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Even if not a partnership, a joint venture carries partnership duties.

Correct. A single purchase for resale is a limited undertaking, so courts may call it a joint venture rather than a partnership (Sandvick v. LaCrosse). Partnership law applies to joint ventures, including the § 409 duties.
They pooled money to buy and resell for a shared profit, which is more than mere co-ownership.
A joint venture may rest on an express or implied contract.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Joint venture

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina each put $100,000 into a joint bank account and use it to buy Mill Creek, a 20-acre parcel, planning to resell it within two years and split the profit equally. They take title in the name "Mill Creek Ventures." They have no written agreement. Cole, who handles zoning, learns from the county planner that the adjoining 10 acres will soon be offered for sale and that combining the two tracts would double Mill Creek's value.

Without telling the others, Cole buys the adjoining 10 acres for himself. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Cole breached his duty of loyalty by secretly taking an opportunity tied to the venture.
Cole breached only his duty of care.
Cole committed no breach, because co-venturers in a single deal owe no fiduciary duties.
Cole committed no breach, because the adjoining land was never venture property.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Opportunities connected to the venture that a co-venturer learns of through his position belong to the venture (Meinhard v. Salmon). As in Sandvick, he had to give the others a chance to participate.
Taking an opportunity for himself is a loyalty breach.
Co-venturers owe "the duty of the finest loyalty" while the enterprise continues (Meinhard).
The duty covers opportunities connected to the venture's business, not just property it already owns.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Taking the venture's opportunity

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina each put $100,000 into a joint bank account and use it to buy Mill Creek, a 20-acre parcel, planning to resell it within two years and split the profit equally. They take title in the name "Mill Creek Ventures." They have no written agreement. Cole, who handles zoning, learns from the county planner that the adjoining 10 acres will soon be offered for sale and that combining the two tracts would double Mill Creek's value.

Which of the following statements about Cole's purchase is true?
o: A court may hold Cole as trustee of the land, or of his profits from it, for the venture.
At a minimum, Cole had to disclose the opportunity so that the others could pursue it.
Cole may keep the land free of any claim if he paid fair market value for it.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A partner or co-venturer must hold as trustee any benefit derived from appropriating an opportunity (§ 409(b)(1)); in Meinhard the court gave Meinhard an interest in the new lease.
True. Meinhard faulted Salmon for keeping the opportunity secret so that Meinhard had no chance to compete for it.
False. Paying a fair price to the seller does not cure taking the venture's opportunity.
Correct. Disclosure was required, and the court may impose a constructive trust.
C is wrong; a fair price to the outside seller is no defense.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Remedy for a taken opportunity

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina each put $100,000 into a joint bank account and use it to buy Mill Creek, a 20-acre parcel, planning to resell it within two years and split the profit equally. They take title in the name "Mill Creek Ventures." They have no written agreement. Cole, who handles zoning, learns from the county planner that the adjoining 10 acres will soon be offered for sale and that combining the two tracts would double Mill Creek's value.

Now assume that the four had signed a written agreement providing: "Each venturer may acquire other real estate for his or her own account, even if it competes with the Venture." Cole uses his own money to buy the adjoining tract. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Cole still breached his duty, because loyalty can never be modified by agreement.
Cole breached his duty unless all the others approved this specific purchase.
Cole committed no breach, and under the clause he may also use the venture's account to fund the purchase.
Cole probably committed no breach, as in Singer, unless he used venture funds or property.
None of the above.
oe: Under RUPA § 105 the agreement may identify permitted activities, if not manifestly unreasonable; it just cannot eliminate loyalty entirely.
The agreement already authorized this type of purchase in advance.
Using venture funds would be taking venture property, which even the Singer clause did not allow.
Correct. In Singer, a clause letting partners compete for their own accounts permitted even "predatory" competition; only taking existing partnership assets or funds would have been a breach.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Contracting around opportunities (Singer)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ana, Ben, Cole, and Dina each put $100,000 into a joint bank account and use it to buy Mill Creek, a 20-acre parcel, planning to resell it within two years and split the profit equally. They take title in the name "Mill Creek Ventures." They have no written agreement. Cole, who handles zoning, learns from the county planner that the adjoining 10 acres will soon be offered for sale and that combining the two tracts would double Mill Creek's value.

The venture hires a surveyor and cannot pay his $8,000 bill. The surveyor sues Dina personally. Dina argues that she was only a passive investor. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dina is not liable, because she took no part in hiring the surveyor or managing the venture.
Dina is personally liable, because partnership liability rules apply to joint ventures.
Dina is liable only up to her $100,000 contribution.
Only Cole is liable, because he handled zoning and hired the surveyor.
None of the above.
oe: Liability flows from her status as a co-owner of the venture, not from participation.
Correct. A joint venture is a partnership for a limited undertaking, and partners are jointly and severally liable for its obligations (RUPA § 306(a)).
Limited liability requires a filed entity such as an LLC, LP, or LLP.
Each co-venturer can bind the venture to ordinary transactions, and all share liability.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Co-venturers' liability

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Delta Seed Co. advances $200,000 to Fiona to finance her farm's growing season. Their written "Crop Financing Agreement" provides that Delta will receive 25% of the crop's net profits, will bear 25% of any net loss, may veto Fiona's choice of crops, and will receive weekly reports. With Delta's approval, Fiona's roadside sign reads "Fiona Farms — in association with Delta Seed."

Fiona's creditors argue that Delta is her partner. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Delta is a lender, because the document is called a "Crop Financing Agreement."
Delta cannot be a partner, because it does not work on the farm.
Delta is probably a partner, because it shares losses as well as profits.
Delta is a partner, because it can veto Fiona's choice of crops.
None of the above.
oe: Labels don't control; courts look at the substance.
A partner may contribute only money; no work is required.

Correct. Sharing in both profits and losses, and acting like a co-owner, tipped Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long toward partnership. In Martin v. Peyton, by contrast, vetoes and information rights were reasonable protections for a loan.
A veto is protective, not management (Martin v. Peyton); the loss sharing is what points toward partnership.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Loss sharing (Kaufman-Brown)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Delta Seed Co. advances $200,000 to Fiona to finance her farm's growing season. Their written "Crop Financing Agreement" provides that Delta will receive 25% of the crop's net profits, will bear 25% of any net loss, may veto Fiona's choice of crops, and will receive weekly reports. With Delta's approval, Fiona's roadside sign reads "Fiona Farms — in association with Delta Seed."

Now assume the agreement gives Delta fixed interest of 8% plus 25% of net profits, says Delta bears no share of any loss, and keeps the veto and weekly reports. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Delta is probably a lender: it bears no losses, and its controls protect its loan.
Delta is a partner, because it receives weekly reports.
Delta is a partner, because any share of profits creates a partnership.
Delta is a partner, because it receives both fixed interest and a share of the profits.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A profit share received as interest or other loan charges does not raise the § 202(c)(3) presumption, and without loss sharing or management power Delta looks like Martin v. Peyton's lenders.
Information rights are routine lender protection.
Profit sharing raises only a presumption, which the loan exception defeats.
Interest, even interest that varies with profits, is a listed exception to the presumption.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Interest on a loan

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Delta Seed Co. advances $200,000 to Fiona to finance her farm's growing season. Their written "Crop Financing Agreement" provides that Delta will receive 25% of the crop's net profits, will bear 25% of any net loss, may veto Fiona's choice of crops, and will receive weekly reports. With Delta's approval, Fiona's roadside sign reads "Fiona Farms — in association with Delta Seed."

A fertilizer supplier reads Fiona's roadside sign and extends her credit, believing that Delta is her partner. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Delta is liable to every Fiona creditor, whether or not it saw the sign.
Delta cannot be liable, because the sign does not use the word "partner."
Delta cannot be liable to the supplier unless it is actually Fiona's partner in the farm.
Delta may be liable as a purported partner, because it consented and the supplier relied.
None of the above.
oe: Liability runs to those who relied on the representation (compare Young v. Jones, where no plaintiff relied).
The question is whether the representation, reasonably read, held Delta out as a partner. Here the supplier read it that way.
Partnership by estoppel creates liability without an actual partnership.

Correct. A person who consents to being represented as a partner is liable to one who, relying on the representation, enters into a transaction with the purported partnership (§ 308(a)). A public representation reaches anyone who relies on it.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Holding out with consent

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Delta Seed Co. advances $200,000 to Fiona to finance her farm's growing season. Their written "Crop Financing Agreement" provides that Delta will receive 25% of the crop's net profits, will bear 25% of any net loss, may veto Fiona's choice of crops, and will receive weekly reports. With Delta's approval, Fiona's roadside sign reads "Fiona Farms — in association with Delta Seed."

Assume Delta is Fiona's partner. The crop fails, and the farm owes outside creditors $100,000 more than its assets. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Delta and Fiona are each personally liable to the outside creditors for the full shortfall.
As between themselves, Delta bears 25% of the loss and Fiona 75%, so a partner who pays more than her share may seek contribution.
Delta's liability to the creditors is capped at 25% of the shortfall because of the agreement.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations (§ 306(a)).
True. The agreed loss shares govern the partners' accounts with each other.
False. An agreement between partners does not limit their liability to outside creditors.
Correct. Liability to outsiders is joint and several; the agreed shares settle accounts between the partners.
C is wrong; the creditors are not bound by the partners' loss-sharing agreement.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Outsiders vs. internal shares

q: A record company privately tells its talent scouts never to promise artists guaranteed payments, although such guarantees are customary in the industry. A scout guarantees payment to a singer anyway, and the company is held bound, as in Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc. Which step would best have protected the company?
o: Nothing; a principal can never limit the customary authority of a role.
Firing the scout after the promise is made.
Telling artists in writing that an officer must approve any guarantee.
Repeating the private instruction to the scouts more firmly, in a signed memo.
None of the above.
oe: It can, by giving third parties notice of the limit.
Firing him does not undo a promise the company is already bound by.

Correct. The problem in Kidd was an uncommunicated, unusual limit on a role whose customary scope included such promises. Notice to third parties, or a countersignature requirement they can see, defeats their reasonable reliance (the casebook's M/M Records problem).
Private instructions limit actual authority only. Third parties without notice may still rely on the role's customary scope.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Guarding against customary authority

q: Under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 219(2), a master may be liable for a servant's tort committed outside the scope of employment when:
o: The master was negligent or reckless.
The master violated a nondelegable duty.
The servant purported to act for the principal and there was reliance on apparent authority, or the servant was aided in accomplishing the tort by the agency relation.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Incomplete. § 219(2)(d) also applies.
Correct. § 219(2) also covers conduct the master intended (§ 219(2)(a)).
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — R2d § 219(2)

q: In Meinhard v. Salmon, why did Salmon owe Meinhard a share of the new lease, even though it would begin only after the venture's original lease ended?
o: It came to Salmon, as manager, during the venture and grew out of it, so he had to disclose it.
Salmon used the venture's funds and credit to obtain the new lease from the landlord.
Meinhard had a contractual right of first refusal on any renewal or extension of the lease.
The court found that Salmon had lied to the landlord.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Cardozo stressed that the new lease was an extension and enlargement of the venture's subject matter offered to the managing co-venturer during the enterprise. At minimum, Salmon had to disclose it so Meinhard could compete.
The breach was the secret taking of the opportunity, not the use of venture funds.
There was no such contract right; the duty came from the fiduciary relationship.
There was no finding of fraud on the landlord.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Meinhard: why Salmon had to disclose

q: Why do real estate developers often use a corporation as the only general partner of a limited partnership?
o: To avoid having to file a certificate of limited partnership with the state.
To give the managers limited liability while keeping pass-through tax treatment.
To turn the limited partners into managers.
To make the LP itself a corporation for state-law purposes.
None of the above.
oe: An LP must file a certificate regardless of who its general partner is.

Correct. The developers own and run the corporate general partner; the corporation, not they, bears general-partner liability, and the LP itself is not taxed at the entity level. Frigidaire v. Union Properties upheld the structure.
The corporate general partner manages; the investors stay limited partners.
The LP stays a partnership; only its general partner is a corporation.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — The corporate general partner

q: Three equal partners each contribute $40,000. In Year 1 the partnership earns $150,000 in profit, and each partner draws $35,000. What is each partner's capital account at the end of Year 1?
o: None of the above.
oe: That subtracts the draw from the contribution but leaves out the $50,000 profit share.
That ignores the profits allocated and the draws taken.
Wrong. $50,000 is each partner's share of the profit, not the account balance; the draws must be subtracted.
That adds the profit share but ignores the $35,000 draw.
Correct. Capital account = contributions + share of profits − share of losses − draws: $40,000 + $50,000 − $35,000 = $55,000, which is not among A–D.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Capital accounts

q: Which of the following arrangements most likely makes a partnership one for a particular undertaking rather than one at will?
o: The partners' shared hope that the business will eventually pay for itself.
The partners' expectation that they will work together for many years.
A partner's loan that the partners agree will be repaid out of profits.
The partnership's purchase of equipment expected to last ten years.
None of the above.
oe: Page v. Page held that a mere common hope of profits does not create a term.
A general expectation of a long relationship is not a definite term or particular undertaking.
Correct. In Owen v. Cohen, an agreement to repay a partner's loan from profits implied that the partnership would last until the loan was repaid.
The useful life of an asset does not set the partnership's term.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Implied term (Owen vs. Page)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sun, Taro, and Uma own Three Rivers Ranch as partners in a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written agreement and share profits equally. Two years ago Uma lent the partnership $200,000 for new barns, on the understanding that the loan would be repaid out of the ranch's profits. Over the past year Taro has threatened the others, refused to sign routine documents, berated Sun in front of the employees, and blocked every land purchase. The ranch's business is at a standstill.

Is Three Rivers Ranch a partnership at will?
o: Probably not; the agreement to repay Uma's loan from profits implies a term.
Yes, because the partners never agreed in writing on a term.
Yes, because, as in Page v. Page, a hope that the business will pay off its debts never creates a term.
No, because every ranch partnership lasts for the life of the land.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Owen v. Cohen, an understanding that a partner's loan will be repaid out of profits implies that the partnership will last at least until repayment.
A term may be implied; no writing is needed.
Page involved only a vague hope that the business would pay for itself; here there is a specific agreement to repay a specific loan from profits.
There is no such rule.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — At will or for a term?

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sun, Taro, and Uma own Three Rivers Ranch as partners in a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written agreement and share profits equally. Two years ago Uma lent the partnership $200,000 for new barns, on the understanding that the loan would be repaid out of the ranch's profits. Over the past year Taro has threatened the others, refused to sign routine documents, berated Sun in front of the employees, and blocked every land purchase. The ranch's business is at a standstill.

Sun and Uma want Taro out of the partnership but want to keep the ranch running. What is their best course under the RUPA?
o: Vote, as a majority of the partners, to expel Taro from the partnership.
Ask a court to expel Taro for making it impracticable to continue with him, then buy him out.
Ask a court to dissolve the partnership, which is the only remedy the RUPA gives for partner misconduct.
Do nothing, because disagreements among partners are never grounds for any remedy.
None of the above.
oe: Without an expulsion clause in the agreement, partners can expel by vote only on the narrow § 601(4) grounds (unlawfulness, transfer of the whole interest, and similar events), none of which applies.

Correct. RUPA § 601(5) permits judicial expulsion on those grounds, as in Giles v. Giles Land Co.; the partnership then buys the dissociated partner's interest under Article 7 instead of selling the land.
Dissolution is available under § 801(4), but RUPA's key innovation is letting the court remove one partner instead.
Ordinary disagreements are not, but conduct like Taro's (threats, abuse, paralysis) is.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Judicial expulsion (Giles)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sun, Taro, and Uma own Three Rivers Ranch as partners in a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written agreement and share profits equally. Two years ago Uma lent the partnership $200,000 for new barns, on the understanding that the loan would be repaid out of the ranch's profits. Over the past year Taro has threatened the others, refused to sign routine documents, berated Sun in front of the employees, and blocked every land purchase. The ranch's business is at a standstill.

Assume the court expels Taro. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Taro's dissociation is wrongful.
Taro may have to wait until the undertaking is completed to be paid, unless he shows that earlier payment will not cause the partnership undue hardship.
Taro is entitled to take part in winding up if the partnership later dissolves.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. In a partnership for a term or particular undertaking, a judicial expulsion before the term ends is a wrongful dissociation (§ 602(b)(2)(ii)).
True. § 701(h). A deferred payment must be secured and bear interest.
False. A partner who dissociated wrongfully may not participate in winding up (§ 802(c)).
Correct. Taro's dissociation is wrongful, so his buyout may be deferred, and he is liable for the damages he caused.
C is wrong; a wrongful dissociator is excluded from winding up.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Consequences of wrongful dissociation

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sun, Taro, and Uma own Three Rivers Ranch as partners in a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written agreement and share profits equally. Two years ago Uma lent the partnership $200,000 for new barns, on the understanding that the loan would be repaid out of the ranch's profits. Over the past year Taro has threatened the others, refused to sign routine documents, berated Sun in front of the employees, and blocked every land purchase. The ranch's business is at a standstill.

Suppose that instead Taro sues to dissolve the partnership, arguing that it is no longer reasonably practicable to carry on the business. The court finds that the impracticability was caused by Taro's own conduct. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The court must order a liquidation sale of the ranch.
Taro has lost both the power and the right to leave.
The court must order dissolution, because impracticability is a ground no matter which partner caused it.
The court is unlikely to dissolve the partnership at the request of the partner who caused the problem.
None of the above.
oe: Nothing requires a sale here, and the court is unlikely to order dissolution at all.
He keeps the power (§ 602(a)); he lacks the right to leave without liability.
Judicial dissolution is equitable, and Collins refused to reward the partner who caused the trouble.

Correct. Collins v. Lewis: there "always exists the power, as opposed to the right," to dissolve; a partner whose own conduct caused the problems cannot obtain an equitable dissolution, and if he leaves anyway he risks damages.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Collins v. Lewis

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sun, Taro, and Uma own Three Rivers Ranch as partners in a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written agreement and share profits equally. Two years ago Uma lent the partnership $200,000 for new barns, on the understanding that the loan would be repaid out of the ranch's profits. Over the past year Taro has threatened the others, refused to sign routine documents, berated Sun in front of the employees, and blocked every land purchase. The ranch's business is at a standstill.

Assume Taro is expelled and Uma's loan has already been repaid, so the partnership owes no debts. The ranch's liquidation value is $3,000,000, and its value as a going concern without Taro is $3,600,000. Taro's wrongful dissociation caused $120,000 in damages. Absent a contrary agreement, what is Taro's buyout price?
o: $880,000, because a wrongful dissociator's interest is valued without goodwill.
$1,080,000, plus interest from the date of dissociation.
$1,200,000, because damages cannot be deducted from the buyout price.
$1,000,000, because buyouts are based on liquidation value.
None of the above.
oe: The UPA excluded goodwill when valuing a wrongful dissolver's interest (§ 38(2)); RUPA § 701 does not.

Correct. The price is what Taro would receive if the assets were sold at the greater of liquidation or going-concern value: one-third of $3,600,000, or $1,200,000, less the $120,000 in damages, plus interest (§ 701(b)–(c)).
Damages for wrongful dissociation are offset against the price (§ 701(c)).
The statute uses the greater of liquidation and going-concern value.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Buyout price (§ 701)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Metro Transit Authority hires BlastCo, an independent demolition contractor, to tear down an old bus terminal on a crowded downtown block. A Metro inspector visits weekly to check progress but does not direct the work. BlastCo's crane operator swings a wrecking ball carelessly, and a wall collapses onto the roof of the neighboring bookstore. Separately, Gus, a BlastCo employee, is injured because BlastCo never gave him a hard hat.

Is Metro likely liable to the bookstore owner?
o: No, because BlastCo is an independent contractor.
No, because Metro's inspector did not direct the work.
Yes, because demolition on a crowded block is inherently dangerous work.
Yes, because every hirer is liable for its contractors' torts.
None of the above.
oe: Non-liability is the general rule, but inherently dangerous work is an exception.
Lack of control defeats the retained-control exception but not the inherently-dangerous exception.

Correct. Majestic Realty v. Toti Contracting: demolition in a built-up area is inherently dangerous unless special precautions are taken, so the party that chose to have the work done bears the risk even though it hired an independent contractor.
The general rule is the opposite; liability here rests on the exception.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Inherently dangerous work (Majestic)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Metro Transit Authority hires BlastCo, an independent demolition contractor, to tear down an old bus terminal on a crowded downtown block. A Metro inspector visits weekly to check progress but does not direct the work. BlastCo's crane operator swings a wrecking ball carelessly, and a wall collapses onto the roof of the neighboring bookstore. Separately, Gus, a BlastCo employee, is injured because BlastCo never gave him a hard hat.

Is Metro likely liable to Gus, BlastCo's injured employee?
o: Probably not, because Gus's injury is generally left to workers' compensation.
Yes, because demolition is inherently dangerous, so Metro answers for every injury on the site.
Yes, because Metro's inspector visited the site every week.
Yes, because Gus may sue anyone who benefits from his work.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum (Posner, J.): the contractor's workers are covered by exclusive workers' compensation, which the principal already pays for in the price, and failing to provide basic safety gear is the contractor's own negligence.
Courts treat the contractor's own employees differently from neighbors, as Anderson explains.
Visiting to check progress is not retaining control over safety equipment.
There is no such rule.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The contractor's own employees (Anderson)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Metro Transit Authority hires BlastCo, an independent demolition contractor, to tear down an old bus terminal on a crowded downtown block. A Metro inspector visits weekly to check progress but does not direct the work. BlastCo's crane operator swings a wrecking ball carelessly, and a wall collapses onto the roof of the neighboring bookstore. Separately, Gus, a BlastCo employee, is injured because BlastCo never gave him a hard hat.

Which additional fact would support Metro's liability to the bookstore even if demolition were not inherently dangerous?
o: Metro hired BlastCo knowing that its license had been suspended for unsafe demolitions.
Metro's inspector ordered BlastCo's crew to swing the wrecking ball the way he chose.
Metro paid BlastCo a fixed price for the job.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. That supports direct liability for negligently selecting an incompetent contractor.
True. A hirer that retains and exercises control over the work answers for harm from that control.
False. Paying by the job points toward independent-contractor status, not liability.
Correct. Negligent selection and retained control are each exceptions to the independent-contractor rule.
C is wrong; it cuts the other way.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Other routes to liability

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Metro Transit Authority hires BlastCo, an independent demolition contractor, to tear down an old bus terminal on a crowded downtown block. A Metro inspector visits weekly to check progress but does not direct the work. BlastCo's crane operator swings a wrecking ball carelessly, and a wall collapses onto the roof of the neighboring bookstore. Separately, Gus, a BlastCo employee, is injured because BlastCo never gave him a hard hat.

Which of the following best explains the general rule that a principal is not liable for an independent contractor's torts?
o: Independent contractors are always required to carry insurance against harm to others.
Hirers never benefit from the work of independent contractors.
Independent contractors are agents who owe the hirer fiduciary duties of loyalty and care in the work.
The hirer cannot control the work, and the contractor can usually take precautions more cheaply.
None of the above.
oe: Insurance is not the rationale, and not all contractors are insured.
They plainly benefit; benefit alone is not the test.
Many independent contractors are not agents at all.
Correct. Vicarious liability tracks the right to control manner and means. The course's "better standard" asks who could prevent the loss most cheaply, which is usually the contractor doing the work.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Why hirers usually aren't liable

q: Which of the following statements about proving an agency relationship is true?
o: The party denying agency must disprove it by clear and convincing evidence.
The party asserting agency must prove it, and may do so circumstantially.
Agency must be proved by a written agreement.
Agency is presumed between spouses who co-own property.
None of the above.
oe: The burden is on the party asserting it.
Correct. The burden is on the party asserting the agency, and it may be shown circumstantially, as in Cargill, where the course of dealing established it.
Agency generally requires no writing.
Botticello v. Stefanovicz rejected that presumption: marriage and co-ownership do not make one spouse the other's agent.
B is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Proving agency

q: Under the Restatement (Third) of Agency, an agent's apparent authority ends:
o: When the principal privately tells the agent that he is fired, whether or not anyone else knows.
One year after the agent's last transaction with the third party.
When the third party can no longer reasonably believe the agent is authorized.
Automatically, when the agent's actual authority ends.
None of the above.
oe: A private firing ends actual authority only; the third party may still reasonably rely.
There is no fixed period; the test is reasonableness.

Correct. R3d § 3.11: apparent authority does not end when actual authority ends; it ends when the third party's belief stops being reasonable, for example after the principal notifies the third party.
Terminating actual authority does not automatically end apparent authority.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — When apparent authority ends

q: A franchisee pays its franchisor royalties equal to 6% of gross sales. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: The royalties do not make the franchisor a partner; gross returns are not profits.
The franchisor is presumed to be a partner, because it shares in the franchisee's revenue.
The franchisor is a partner, because it licenses its trademarks to the franchisee.
The franchisor is a partner only if the franchise agreement calls it one.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 202(c)(2): sharing gross returns does not by itself establish a partnership, and a franchisor is distinguished from a partner in the "partnership v. everybody" analysis.
The presumption arises from sharing profits, not gross revenue.
A trademark license is a contract, not co-ownership of the business.
Labels don't control, and nothing here suggests co-ownership.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Royalties on gross sales

q: Under the RUPA, the obligation of good faith and fair dealing:
o: Cannot be eliminated by the agreement, though it may set reasonable standards for it.
May be waived entirely in a written partnership agreement.
Requires each partner to put the partnership's interests ahead of his own in every matter.
Applies only after the partnership dissolves.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Partners must discharge their duties consistently with the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing (§ 409(d)). The agreement may prescribe standards that are not manifestly unreasonable, but may not eliminate the obligation (§ 105).
It is one of the terms § 105 protects from elimination.
A partner does not breach any duty merely because his conduct furthers his own interest (§ 409(e)).
It applies throughout the partnership.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Good faith and fair dealing

q: Under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001), a limited partner:
o: Becomes personally liable if she gives the general partner business advice.
Owes no fiduciary duty solely because she is a limited partner.
Is an agent of the partnership who can bind it to contracts.
Owes the same duty of loyalty as a general partner.
None of the above.
oe: Under ULPA (2001) § 303, a limited partner is not liable for the LP's obligations even if she participates in management.

Correct. ULPA § 305: a limited partner does not have any fiduciary duty to the LP or any other partner solely by reason of being a limited partner (though she must act consistently with good faith and fair dealing). That is why a limited partner may run a competing business.
A limited partner is not an agent of the LP solely by being a limited partner.
The general partner owes loyalty (ULPA § 408); a limited partner does not, merely as a limited partner.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Limited partners' duties

q: A partnership's buyout agreement covers death, disability, and retirement only. A partner divorces, and the divorce court awards half of her transferable interest to her ex-spouse. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership dissolves.
The ex-spouse becomes a partner with full management rights in place of the divorced partner.
The ex-spouse is a transferee with distribution rights only, so a divorce trigger was needed.
The divorce automatically triggers a buyout at book value under the RUPA's default rules.
None of the above.
oe: A transfer of a transferable interest is not even a dissociation, let alone a dissolution.
Admission as a partner requires the consent of the partners (§ 402); a transfer passes only economic rights.

Correct. A transferee gets distributions only (RUPA § 503). Without a divorce trigger, the ex-spouse may be stuck with an illiquid interest and the partners with an unwanted outsider. Alaska Plastics, which the slide cites, is the cautionary tale.
The agreement has no divorce trigger, and no statute supplies one.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — The missing divorce trigger

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ellis and Fay formed E&F Builders, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), in 2020, with no fixed term. Their written agreement provides: "If a partner withdraws, the partnership shall continue, and it shall buy the withdrawing partner's interest under Article 7." In 2022 the firm borrowed $200,000 from First Bank. In 2023 Gwen was admitted as a partner and contributed $50,000. In 2024 Ellis withdrew. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation and never told its suppliers, and Ellis's name stayed painted on the firm's trucks. In 2025 the firm signed a supply contract with Stoneworks, which did not know that Ellis had left.

E&F Builders defaults on the 2022 First Bank loan, and the partnership's assets run out. Who is personally liable to First Bank for the balance?
o: Ellis, Fay, and Gwen, because all of them are now partners in the partnership that owes the debt.
Only Fay, because Ellis left and Gwen joined after the loan.
Ellis and Fay, but not Gwen, although Gwen's contribution can be used to pay the bank.
No one, because the bank must look only to the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Gwen was admitted after the loan was made, so § 306(b) protects her personal assets.
Ellis remains liable for obligations incurred while he was a partner.

Correct. Ellis and Fay were partners when the loan was made, and Ellis's later dissociation does not discharge his liability (§ 703(a)). An incoming partner is not personally liable for obligations incurred before admission (§ 306(b)), but what she contributed belongs to the partnership and is reachable.
Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations once partnership assets are exhausted (§§ 306–307).
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Old debts and a new partner

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ellis and Fay formed E&F Builders, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), in 2020, with no fixed term. Their written agreement provides: "If a partner withdraws, the partnership shall continue, and it shall buy the withdrawing partner's interest under Article 7." In 2022 the firm borrowed $200,000 from First Bank. In 2023 Gwen was admitted as a partner and contributed $50,000. In 2024 Ellis withdrew. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation and never told its suppliers, and Ellis's name stayed painted on the firm's trucks. In 2025 the firm signed a supply contract with Stoneworks, which did not know that Ellis had left.

Is Ellis personally liable on the 2025 Stoneworks contract?
o: No, because a dissociated partner is never liable for obligations incurred after he leaves.
He may be, because it was within two years and Stoneworks reasonably thought he was a partner.
No, because the partnership bought out his interest.
Yes, for every obligation the firm ever incurs, because his name is still on the trucks.
None of the above.
oe: The two-year rule of § 703(b) is an exception.

Correct. A dissociated partner is liable for a partnership obligation incurred within two years after dissociation if the other party reasonably believed he was a partner and did not know or have notice of the dissociation (§ 703(b)). His name on the trucks and the firm's failure to file or give notice support Stoneworks.
A buyout between the partners does not give outsiders notice.
Liability is limited to the § 703(b) window and to creditors who lack notice.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Lingering liability (§ 703)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ellis and Fay formed E&F Builders, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), in 2020, with no fixed term. Their written agreement provides: "If a partner withdraws, the partnership shall continue, and it shall buy the withdrawing partner's interest under Article 7." In 2022 the firm borrowed $200,000 from First Bank. In 2023 Gwen was admitted as a partner and contributed $50,000. In 2024 Ellis withdrew. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation and never told its suppliers, and Ellis's name stayed painted on the firm's trucks. In 2025 the firm signed a supply contract with Stoneworks, which did not know that Ellis had left.

What was the effect of Ellis's withdrawal in 2024?
o: Ellis was dissociated, and the partnership continued and had to buy his interest.
Ellis did not dissociate until he was paid for his interest.
Ellis's withdrawal was wrongful, because the partnership continued without him.
The partnership dissolved, because a withdrawal from an at-will partnership always causes dissolution.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Without the clause, a partner's express will to withdraw from an at-will partnership would dissolve it (§ 801(1)). But the agreement may change § 801(1)–(3); among the dissolution events, § 105(c) protects only § 801(4)–(5). So the § 603 switch sends the case to an Article 7 buyout.
Dissociation occurs on notice of his express will (§ 601(1)); payment comes afterward.
The partnership had no term, and Ellis breached no express provision, so his withdrawal was rightful (§ 602(b)).
§ 801(1) is a default rule the agreement may change.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Contracting around at-will dissolution

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ellis and Fay formed E&F Builders, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), in 2020, with no fixed term. Their written agreement provides: "If a partner withdraws, the partnership shall continue, and it shall buy the withdrawing partner's interest under Article 7." In 2022 the firm borrowed $200,000 from First Bank. In 2023 Gwen was admitted as a partner and contributed $50,000. In 2024 Ellis withdrew. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation and never told its suppliers, and Ellis's name stayed painted on the firm's trucks. In 2025 the firm signed a supply contract with Stoneworks, which did not know that Ellis had left.

Ellis and the partnership cannot agree on the price of his interest. Which of the following statements is true?
o: If they reach no agreement within 90 days after Ellis's written demand, the partnership must pay him its estimate of the price plus interest.
Ellis must wait until the partnership eventually dissolves and winds up to be paid.
Ellis is entitled only to the return of his original capital contribution.
The partnership may pay Ellis whatever it chooses, because the agreement does not set a price.
None of the above.
oe: Wrong. The period is 120 days, not 90 (§ 701(e)).
Deferral applies only to a partner who wrongfully dissociates before the end of a term (§ 701(h)).
The § 701 price is based on the greater of liquidation and going-concern value.
Without an agreed price, § 701(b) supplies the formula.

Correct. If no agreement is reached within 120 days after Ellis's written demand, the partnership must pay him its estimate of the buyout price plus interest (§ 701(e)). Ellis left rightfully, so he need not wait for any term to end, and he may sue within 120 days after the tender to have a court set the price (§ 701(i)). None of A–D states this.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Buyout timing (§ 701)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ellis and Fay formed E&F Builders, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), in 2020, with no fixed term. Their written agreement provides: "If a partner withdraws, the partnership shall continue, and it shall buy the withdrawing partner's interest under Article 7." In 2022 the firm borrowed $200,000 from First Bank. In 2023 Gwen was admitted as a partner and contributed $50,000. In 2024 Ellis withdrew. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation and never told its suppliers, and Ellis's name stayed painted on the firm's trucks. In 2025 the firm signed a supply contract with Stoneworks, which did not know that Ellis had left.

Which of the following steps would have protected E&F Builders against obligations Ellis or his name might create after he left?
o: Filing a statement of dissociation, which gives outsiders constructive notice 90 days after it takes effect.
Notifying its regular suppliers that Ellis had left.
Getting Ellis's private promise not to deal with the firm's suppliers.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A third party who knows or has notice of the dissociation cannot rely on § 702 or § 703. It would also have helped to paint over his name.
Not protection against third parties. A private promise gives outsiders no notice, though Ellis would be liable to the firm for any loss he caused (§ 702(b)).
Correct. Filing and direct notice both cut off lingering authority and liability.
C does not protect the firm against third parties.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — What the firm should have done

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Restwell Inns franchises hotels. Its franchise agreement requires every franchisee to use Restwell's own electronic key-card system, which Restwell installs and maintains remotely, and to follow Restwell's security manual, which sets the number of night guards. Restwell does not hire, pay, or supervise franchisee employees, set room rates, or handle daily maintenance. Every sign, towel, and web page says only "Restwell Inns." At a Restwell Inn owned by the franchisee Kimball Hospitality, an intruder uses a defective key card to enter a room and assaults a guest, Lane, who chose the hotel because of Restwell's reputation for safety.

Lane sues Restwell. Under the majority test of Kerl v. Rasmussen, could Restwell be vicariously liable?
o: No, because Restwell does not hire, train, or supervise any of Kimball's hotel employees.
Yes, because the hotel carries the Restwell brand.
No, because a franchisor is never liable for injuries at a franchised location.
Yes, possibly, because Restwell controlled the key-card system that caused the harm.
None of the above.
oe: That decided Kerl, where the harm came from hiring and supervision. Here the harm came from something Restwell itself controlled.
Branding alone is not control (Murphy v. Holiday Inns).
Kerl states a test, not an immunity.

Correct. A franchisor is vicariously liable only if it controls, or has the right to control, the daily operation of the specific aspect of the franchisee's business that caused the harm (Kerl). Restwell installed and maintains the key cards and sets security staffing.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Control of the instrumentality (Kerl)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Restwell Inns franchises hotels. Its franchise agreement requires every franchisee to use Restwell's own electronic key-card system, which Restwell installs and maintains remotely, and to follow Restwell's security manual, which sets the number of night guards. Restwell does not hire, pay, or supervise franchisee employees, set room rates, or handle daily maintenance. Every sign, towel, and web page says only "Restwell Inns." At a Restwell Inn owned by the franchisee Kimball Hospitality, an intruder uses a defective key card to enter a room and assaults a guest, Lane, who chose the hotel because of Restwell's reputation for safety.

Suppose instead that Lane had slipped on a wet lobby floor that Kimball's staff failed to mop. Would Restwell likely be vicariously liable?
o: Yes, because franchisors are strictly liable for their franchisees.
Yes, because Restwell inspects its franchised hotels.
No, because Restwell has no control over daily maintenance.
Yes, because Restwell's manual governs security at the hotel.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such rule.
Inspections to protect the brand are not control of daily operations.

Correct. Murphy v. Holiday Inns: the franchisor's rules for system-wide uniformity did not give it control over daily maintenance, so there was no agency. Under Kerl, Restwell did not control the aspect that caused this harm.
Control over security says nothing about mopping floors; Kerl looks at the specific aspect that caused the harm.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Brand standards are not control (Murphy)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Restwell Inns franchises hotels. Its franchise agreement requires every franchisee to use Restwell's own electronic key-card system, which Restwell installs and maintains remotely, and to follow Restwell's security manual, which sets the number of night guards. Restwell does not hire, pay, or supervise franchisee employees, set room rates, or handle daily maintenance. Every sign, towel, and web page says only "Restwell Inns." At a Restwell Inn owned by the franchisee Kimball Hospitality, an intruder uses a defective key card to enter a room and assaults a guest, Lane, who chose the hotel because of Restwell's reputation for safety.

Lane also argues that Restwell is liable under an apparent-agency theory, as in Miller v. McDonald's Corp. Which of the following supports that argument?
o: Restwell held Kimball out as its agent through uniform branding that never disclosed independent ownership.
Lane chose the hotel because of Restwell's reputation for safety.
Restwell controlled Kimball's hiring of night guards.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The representation element of R2d § 267.
True. That is justifiable reliance on the apparent principal's care or skill.
False, and not required. Apparent agency rests on representation and reliance, not on actual control.
Correct. Holding out plus justifiable reliance supports apparent agency, as in Miller, where the customer chose McDonald's for its reputation.
C is not true on these facts and is not an element of apparent agency.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Apparent agency (Miller)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Restwell Inns franchises hotels. Its franchise agreement requires every franchisee to use Restwell's own electronic key-card system, which Restwell installs and maintains remotely, and to follow Restwell's security manual, which sets the number of night guards. Restwell does not hire, pay, or supervise franchisee employees, set room rates, or handle daily maintenance. Every sign, towel, and web page says only "Restwell Inns." At a Restwell Inn owned by the franchisee Kimball Hospitality, an intruder uses a defective key card to enter a room and assaults a guest, Lane, who chose the hotel because of Restwell's reputation for safety.

Which of the following statements about Kimball Hospitality is most accurate?
o: Kimball cannot be liable if Restwell is liable.
Kimball may be directly liable for its own negligence, such as understaffing night guards.
Kimball is liable only if Restwell is not.
Kimball can avoid liability because the franchise agreement makes Restwell responsible for security.
None of the above.
oe: More than one party can be liable for the same harm.
Correct. A franchisee runs its own business and answers for its own negligence, whatever the franchisor's liability.
Their liabilities are not alternatives.
A contract between Restwell and Kimball does not bind Lane.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The franchisee's own liability

q: Ann manages an apartment building for its owner, Paul. Paul tells her, "Do not hire a janitor." Resident managers customarily hire janitors, and Ann hires one from CleanCo, which knows nothing of Paul's instruction. Which of the following statements is true?
o: No actual authority, but Paul may be bound if CleanCo reasonably relied on Ann's position.
Ann had implied actual authority, because local custom allows resident managers to hire janitors.
Paul cannot be bound, because Ann disobeyed a direct order.
Ann had express authority, because she was hired to manage the building.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The casebook's apartment-manager hypo: Paul's express instruction controls between Paul and Ann, so there is no actual authority. But placing Ann in a role that customarily carries this power is a manifestation to third parties, who need not inquire about secret limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
Custom can supply implied authority only when the principal has not said otherwise. An express instruction controls.
Disobedience ends actual authority, not necessarily apparent authority.
Express authority covers what the principal actually said, and Paul said the opposite.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Told not to hire, but custom allows

q: Restatement (Third) of Agency § 7.07 was written in part to fix which problem with the Restatement (Second)'s scope-of-employment test?
o: The Second Restatement excluded every intentional tort, however job-related, from the scope of employment.
The Second Restatement ignored the employee's purpose.
The Second Restatement made employers liable for everything their employees did.
Its time-and-space test fits poorly for professionals who work at no fixed time or place.
None of the above.
oe: It did not; R2d § 228(1)(d) covers intentional force that is not unexpectable, and §§ 230–231 cover forbidden and even criminal acts.
Purpose to serve the master is one of the § 228 requirements.
