It limited liability to conduct within scope.

Correct. R3d § 7.07 asks instead whether the employee was doing assigned work or a course of conduct subject to the employer's control, and treats as outside scope only an independent course of conduct not intended to serve any purpose of the employer.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Why the R3d rewrote scope

q: Partner Kay buys a building with her own money and takes title in her own name, without any reference to the partnership. The partnership uses the building as its office. Under RUPA § 204, the building is:
o: Owned by the partners as tenants in partnership.
Presumed to be Kay's separate property, even though the partnership uses it.
Conclusively partnership property, because Kay is a partner.
Presumed to be partnership property, because the partnership uses it.
None of the above.
oe: That is the UPA (1914) concept, and it applied only to partnership property.

Correct. Property acquired in a partner's name, without an indication of partnership capacity and without partnership funds, is presumed to be the partner's separate property even if used for partnership purposes (§ 204(d)).
Partners may own property separately; intent at acquisition controls.
Use alone does not make property the partnership's.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Property in a partner's own name

q: In Meehan v. Shaughnessy, the departing partners had unfairly obtained client consents to move cases to their new firm. What did the court require?
o: The departing partners had to give up every client they had ever served.
No remedy, because partners may always leave and take clients.
They had to prove the clients would have come anyway, or hold those profits in trust.
The old firm had to prove the exact damages caused by each client's departure to the new firm.
None of the above.
oe: The remedy was tied to the cases whose consents were unfairly obtained.
Preparing to leave was permitted, but the way they solicited clients was not.

Correct. Because they breached loyalty in how they got the consents, the burden shifted to them to show the clients would have consented to removal in any event; otherwise they held the profits in constructive trust.
The court shifted the burden to the fiduciaries who breached.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Meehan: burden on remedy

q: Under the ULLCA, when an LLC member transfers her transferable interest to an outsider:
o: The transferee gets the member's distributions, but no role in management.
The transfer is void unless all members consent.
The transferee becomes a member with full management and information rights.
The LLC must dissolve.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A transferee has only economic rights (§ 502); management and information rights stay with the member, who remains a member unless dissociated.
Transfers of transferable interests are generally permitted; consent is needed for admission as a member.
Becoming a member requires admission under the operating agreement or with the consent of all members.
A transfer is not a dissolution event.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC transferee

q: Which of the following describes "affirmative" asset partitioning (entity shielding)?
o: Shielding the owners' personal assets from the firm's creditors.
Taxing the firm's income at the entity level.
Separating the firm's managers from its owners.
Shielding the firm's assets from the claims of the owners' personal creditors.
None of the above.
oe: That is defensive partitioning, which is what we call limited liability.
Tax treatment is a separate question.
That is about governance, not assets.
Correct. Affirmative partitioning protects the firm's assets for the firm's creditors; for example, a partner's personal creditor gets only a charging order, not the firm's property.
D is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Affirmative asset partitioning

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Rivera Apartments, L.P. files a certificate of limited partnership naming Rivera GP, Inc., a corporation owned and run by Sam, as its only general partner. Tia and Uma each invest $500,000 as limited partners. Uma also works part time as the LP's leasing consultant and attends its monthly management meetings. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may not borrow more than $1,000,000 without the limited partners' consent. It says nothing about competition.

Rivera Apartments defaults on a supplier's contract. The supplier argues that Uma, who attends management meetings and works as leasing consultant, is personally liable. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Uma is liable as a general partner, because she took part in control of the business.
Uma is liable up to twice her investment.
Uma is not liable for the LP's obligations, even though she participates in management.
Uma is liable, because working for the LP makes her its employee.
None of the above.
oe: That was the old control rule, which ULPA (2001) eliminated.
There is no such rule.

Correct. Under ULPA (2001) § 303, a limited partner is not personally liable for the LP's obligations solely by reason of being a limited partner, even if she participates in the management and control of the LP. The old "control rule" is largely gone.
Even if she is an employee, an employee is not liable for the employer's contracts.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — No control rule

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Rivera Apartments, L.P. files a certificate of limited partnership naming Rivera GP, Inc., a corporation owned and run by Sam, as its only general partner. Tia and Uma each invest $500,000 as limited partners. Uma also works part time as the LP's leasing consultant and attends its monthly management meetings. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may not borrow more than $1,000,000 without the limited partners' consent. It says nothing about competition.

Tia, without telling Sam, builds a competing apartment complex across the street. Rivera GP sues her for breach of the duty of loyalty. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Tia breached a duty to disclose her new business to the general partner.
No breach, because a limited partner owes no fiduciary duty just by being one.
Tia breached her duty of loyalty by competing with the partnership.
Tia breached her duty of care by causing the partnership to lose tenants.
None of the above.
oe: A limited partner has no such duty merely because she is a limited partner.
Correct. ULPA § 305. The general partner owes loyalty; a passive investor may run a competing business, as the professor's sample exam also concludes.
That duty binds general partners, not limited partners as such.
A limited partner owes no duty of care as such.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — A limited partner competes

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Rivera Apartments, L.P. files a certificate of limited partnership naming Rivera GP, Inc., a corporation owned and run by Sam, as its only general partner. Tia and Uma each invest $500,000 as limited partners. Uma also works part time as the LP's leasing consultant and attends its monthly management meetings. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may not borrow more than $1,000,000 without the limited partners' consent. It says nothing about competition.

Sam, acting for Rivera GP, signs a $2,000,000 construction loan with Coast Bank without the limited partners' consent. Coast Bank never saw the partnership agreement. Is the LP bound?
o: Yes, because the loan was in the ordinary course and the bank had no notice of the limit.
No, because the partnership agreement capped the general partner's borrowing at $1,000,000.
No, because a lender is charged with knowledge of the partnership agreement.
Yes, but only if the limited partners later ratify the loan.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. RNR Investments v. Peoples First Community Bank: under ULPA § 402, which parallels RUPA § 301, a general partner's ordinary-course act binds the LP unless the third party knew or had notice of the lack of authority. Banks have no duty to read partnership agreements.
The cap limits actual authority, not the power to bind a third party without notice.
RNR rejected that argument.
No ratification is needed.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — General partner's authority (RNR)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Rivera Apartments, L.P. files a certificate of limited partnership naming Rivera GP, Inc., a corporation owned and run by Sam, as its only general partner. Tia and Uma each invest $500,000 as limited partners. Uma also works part time as the LP's leasing consultant and attends its monthly management meetings. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may not borrow more than $1,000,000 without the limited partners' consent. It says nothing about competition.

The LP cannot repay Coast Bank. The bank sues Sam personally, arguing that he controls the general partner. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Sam is personally liable as a general partner, because he makes the decisions.
Sam is liable for any amount that exceeds the LP's assets.
Sam is not personally liable just because he runs the corporate general partner.
Sam is liable because a corporation cannot serve as a general partner.
None of the above.
oe: The general partner is the corporation, not Sam.
That would erase the point of the corporate general partner.

Correct. Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties: individuals who acted only as officers of a corporate general partner, dealing with a creditor that knew it was dealing with the corporation, were not personally liable.
A corporation may be a general partner; it is a common structure.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Frigidaire

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Rivera Apartments, L.P. files a certificate of limited partnership naming Rivera GP, Inc., a corporation owned and run by Sam, as its only general partner. Tia and Uma each invest $500,000 as limited partners. Uma also works part time as the LP's leasing consultant and attends its monthly management meetings. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may not borrow more than $1,000,000 without the limited partners' consent. It says nothing about competition.

Now suppose that Sam never filed the certificate of limited partnership, though everyone signed a written agreement naming Tia and Uma as limited partners. Rivera then runs up large debts. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Tia and Uma cannot be liable, because they contributed only capital.
Tia and Uma are liable only up to their capital contributions.
Tia and Uma remain limited partners, because the written agreement sets out their status.
Tia and Uma may be treated as general partners, personally liable for the debts.
None of the above.
oe: Contributing only capital does not shield a partner in a general partnership.
That is the limited-partner shield, which never came into being.
The private agreement cannot create limited liability that requires a state filing.

Correct. A limited partnership comes into existence only when its certificate is filed. Without it, co-owners of a business for profit are a general partnership, and the "limited" partners may be treated as general partners, the answer the professor's sample exam gives.
D is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — No certificate filed

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Professor Paula is writing a book. She tells her research assistant, Allie, "Hire a typist for my manuscript. Pay no more than $9 an hour." The going rate for typists in town is $10 an hour. Allie posts an ad on the university job board, signed "Allie, for Professor Paula," and hires Zelda at $10 an hour. Zelda knows nothing about the $9 limit.

Did Allie have actual authority to hire Zelda at $10 an hour?
o: Yes, because custom sets the rate at $10, which gives Allie implied authority.
No, because Paula's express instruction capped the rate at $9.
Yes, because Paula expressly authorized her to hire a typist.
Yes, because $10 is the going rate, so the hire was reasonable.
None of the above.
oe: Custom fills gaps in the principal's instructions; it cannot override an express limit.
Correct. Actual authority turns on what the agent reasonably understands from the principal's manifestations, and Paula expressly set a $9 cap.
She was authorized to hire, but only at $9 or less.
Reasonableness does not create actual authority the principal withheld.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Express limit controls actual authority

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Professor Paula is writing a book. She tells her research assistant, Allie, "Hire a typist for my manuscript. Pay no more than $9 an hour." The going rate for typists in town is $10 an hour. Allie posts an ad on the university job board, signed "Allie, for Professor Paula," and hires Zelda at $10 an hour. Zelda knows nothing about the $9 limit.

Zelda types the manuscript and bills Paula at $10 an hour. Is Paula likely bound to pay $10?
o: Probably yes, because Zelda had no notice of the secret limit and was hired at the going rate.
No, because only Allie's own ad, not Paula, said Allie acted for Paula.
No, because Allie lacked actual authority to pay more than $9 an hour, and Zelda bears that risk.
Yes, but only at $9, with Zelda bearing the rest.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. This is the casebook's research-assistant problem. Paula authorized Allie to deal with typists on her behalf, and a typist reasonably expects such an agent to be able to pay the going rate. As in Kidd v. Edison, an uncommunicated limit does not bind a third party without notice.
Paula authorized Allie to recruit for her, so the ad is within what Paula authorized Allie to say.
Lack of actual authority is not the end; apparent or customary authority may bind Paula.
If Paula is bound, she is bound to the contract as made.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Secret limits and the going rate

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Professor Paula is writing a book. She tells her research assistant, Allie, "Hire a typist for my manuscript. Pay no more than $9 an hour." The going rate for typists in town is $10 an hour. Allie posts an ad on the university job board, signed "Allie, for Professor Paula," and hires Zelda at $10 an hour. Zelda knows nothing about the $9 limit.

Suppose instead that Paula had told Allie only, "Find typist candidates and send them to me; I will do the hiring," and Allie hired Zelda anyway. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Paula is bound, because authority to find candidates implies authority to hire one of them.
Paula is not bound unless she ratifies, because Allie had no authority to hire.
Zelda's only remedy is against the university.
Paula is bound, because Zelda was hired at the going rate.
None of the above.
oe: Hiring is the very decision Paula kept for herself.
Correct. The casebook's answer: an agent sent only to find candidates has no authority to hire, and recruiting candidates is not a role that customarily includes hiring.
The university is not a party; Zelda's claims run against Paula (if she ratifies) or Allie.
The rate is irrelevant if Allie had no authority to hire at all.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — No authority to hire at all

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Professor Paula is writing a book. She tells her research assistant, Allie, "Hire a typist for my manuscript. Pay no more than $9 an hour." The going rate for typists in town is $10 an hour. Allie posts an ad on the university job board, signed "Allie, for Professor Paula," and hires Zelda at $10 an hour. Zelda knows nothing about the $9 limit.

Return to the original facts, where Paula said "no more than $9 an hour." Which of the following statements about Allie is true?
o: Allie breached her duty to obey Paula's instructions.
If Paula has to pay the extra $1 an hour, Allie may be liable to her for that loss.
If Paula ratifies the hire knowing all the facts, Allie is relieved of liability for exceeding her authority.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. An agent must act only within actual authority and follow the principal's lawful instructions (R3d § 8.09).
True. An agent is liable for losses caused by acting beyond her authority.
True. Ratification gives the act the effect of actual authority and relieves the agent of liability to the principal for exceeding it.
Incomplete. Ratification would also relieve Allie of liability.
Correct. Allie breached her duty and may owe Paula the difference, unless Paula ratifies with full knowledge.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — An agent who exceeds instructions

q: Which of the following creates liability by operation of law, rather than by the acts or agreement of the parties?
o: Ratification.
An implied agreement.
Estoppel.
An express agreement.
The principal's conduct that leads a third party to believe the agent is authorized.
oe: Ratification is the principal's own later affirmance.
An implied agreement is still the parties' own act, shown by conduct.

Correct. The course divides the modes of creating an agency into the parties' own acts or omissions (express or implied agreement, conduct leading a third party to believe, ratification) and operation of law (estoppel, statute).
An express agreement is the parties' own act.
That is apparent authority, which rests on the principal's own manifestation.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Agency by operation of law

q: An undisclosed principal generally may enforce a contract its agent made with a third party. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The principal may not enforce the contract if its terms exclude an undisclosed principal.
The principal may not enforce the contract if its existence was fraudulently concealed, for example by the agent's lying when asked whether he acted for that principal.
The third party may assert set-offs it had against the agent before learning of the principal.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The parties may contract to deal only with each other.
True. Fraudulent concealment of the principal is a recognized exception.
True. A third party who dealt with the agent as the principal keeps defenses it acquired before learning of the principal.
Incomplete. The set-off rule is also true.
Correct. The third party is liable to the undisclosed principal unless the contract excludes it or its existence was fraudulently concealed, and the third party keeps its set-offs.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal enforcing a contract

q: Under the RUPA's default rules, a partner who spends six months winding up the partnership's business is entitled to:
o: Reasonable compensation for her services in winding up the business.
A double share of the remaining assets.
Nothing, because partners are never paid for their services.
A salary equal to what she earned from profits in the best year.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A partner is not entitled to pay for services performed for the partnership, except reasonable compensation for winding up its business (§ 401(j)).
Distributions follow § 806, not the work done in winding up.
Winding up is the statutory exception to the no-compensation rule.
The statute provides only reasonable compensation.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Pay for winding up

q: A partnership files a statement of partnership authority that GRANTS partner Cruz authority to sign contracts of up to $500,000 for the partnership. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: The grant is ineffective until it is recorded in the county land records.
It is conclusive for a person who gives value relying on it without contrary knowledge.
The grant binds only the partners, not third parties.
The grant limits every other partner's authority to $500,000 too.
None of the above.
oe: Recording matters only for authority to transfer real property.

Correct. A filed grant of authority is conclusive in favor of a person who is not a partner and gives value without knowledge that the partner lacks authority (§ 303(d)), even though filed limits are generally not notice to third parties.
Its purpose is to let third parties rely on it.
A grant to one partner does not limit the others.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Filed grant of authority

q: In Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States, Judge Friendly suggested that the government would NOT have been liable if the drunk sailor had:
o: Shot a security guard who was his wife's lover.
Set fire to a bar on shore while returning to the ship.
Turned the wheels that flooded the drydock while returning to his ship.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Conduct arising from the sailor's personal or domestic life is not a risk characteristic of the enterprise.
True. Risks no different from those the community faces generally are not characteristic of the employer's activities.
False. That is what happened, and the government was liable.
Correct. Bushey's enterprise-risk test excludes purely personal acts and risks the community faces anyway.
C describes the case itself, where the government was liable.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Limits of Bushey

q: Under the ULLCA, which of the following does NOT cause an LLC to dissolve?
o: An event the operating agreement says causes dissolution.
The consent of all the members.
A member's dissociation.
The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the LLC has no members.
A court order on a member's application, for example because the LLC's business is unlawful.
oe: A dissolution event (§ 701).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
Correct: this does not dissolve the LLC. A member's dissociation leaves the LLC in place; the dissociated member holds her interest as a transferee (§ 603).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
topic: 14 · LLCs — Not a dissolution event

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Prairie CPA Partners is a general partnership of five accountants governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Its managing partner, Yuri, invests the firm's $2,000,000 cash reserve in a bond fund after reading the fund's prospectus and consulting the firm's banker. The fund collapses, and the firm loses $1,200,000. Zoe, a partner who works at the firm's satellite office, asks to see the firm's books and the investment file. The partnership agreement provides: "A partner may inspect the books only with the managing partner's approval." Abe, a partner who retired two years ago and is paid under a retirement agreement, also wants to sue Yuri.

The other partners claim that Yuri breached his duty of care. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Probably not, because at most he was negligent, which is not a breach under the RUPA.
Yuri breached his duty, because a partner must act as a prudent investor would.
Yuri breached his duty, because the investment lost money.
Yuri breached his duty of loyalty.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 409(c). Yuri read the prospectus and consulted the banker; at most this was ordinary negligence, which is not a breach (compare the business judgment rule in Bane v. Ferguson).
The RUPA standard is far lower than ordinary prudence.
A bad outcome is not a breach of the duty of care.
Nothing suggests he had a conflict of interest or took a personal benefit.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Duty of care

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Prairie CPA Partners is a general partnership of five accountants governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Its managing partner, Yuri, invests the firm's $2,000,000 cash reserve in a bond fund after reading the fund's prospectus and consulting the firm's banker. The fund collapses, and the firm loses $1,200,000. Zoe, a partner who works at the firm's satellite office, asks to see the firm's books and the investment file. The partnership agreement provides: "A partner may inspect the books only with the managing partner's approval." Abe, a partner who retired two years ago and is paid under a retirement agreement, also wants to sue Yuri.

Under the RUPA, the partnership and Yuri must provide Zoe with which of the following?
o: Without demand, any information about the partnership's business and affairs reasonably required for the proper exercise of her rights and duties.
On demand, any other information about the partnership's business and affairs, unless the demand or the information demanded is unreasonable or otherwise improper.
Access to the partnership's books and records.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A partnership must give partners access to its books and records (§ 408(a)).
Incomplete. The right of access to books and records is also part of a partner's information rights.
Correct. A partner gets access to the books, the information she needs without asking, and other information on demand.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Information rights

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Prairie CPA Partners is a general partnership of five accountants governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Its managing partner, Yuri, invests the firm's $2,000,000 cash reserve in a bond fund after reading the fund's prospectus and consulting the firm's banker. The fund collapses, and the firm loses $1,200,000. Zoe, a partner who works at the firm's satellite office, asks to see the firm's books and the investment file. The partnership agreement provides: "A partner may inspect the books only with the managing partner's approval." Abe, a partner who retired two years ago and is paid under a retirement agreement, also wants to sue Yuri.

Yuri refuses Zoe's request, pointing to the clause requiring his approval for any inspection. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Zoe must dissociate before she can see the books.
The clause is fully enforceable, because the information rules are default rules.
The clause is void only as to the managing partner.
It is unenforceable insofar as it unreasonably restricts Zoe's right to information.
None of the above.
oe: A partner, not a former partner, has the strongest information rights.
Information rights are among the protected terms that an agreement cannot unreasonably restrict.
The clause restricts the other partners, and that is the problem.
Correct. The partnership agreement may not unreasonably restrict a partner's right to information under § 408, though it may impose reasonable restrictions on its availability and use (§ 105(c)).
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Restricting information rights

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Prairie CPA Partners is a general partnership of five accountants governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Its managing partner, Yuri, invests the firm's $2,000,000 cash reserve in a bond fund after reading the fund's prospectus and consulting the firm's banker. The fund collapses, and the firm loses $1,200,000. Zoe, a partner who works at the firm's satellite office, asks to see the firm's books and the investment file. The partnership agreement provides: "A partner may inspect the books only with the managing partner's approval." Abe, a partner who retired two years ago and is paid under a retirement agreement, also wants to sue Yuri.

Can Abe, the retired partner, recover from Yuri for the loss?
o: Yes, because a partnership owes retired partners the same duties it owes current partners.
Probably not, because partners owe no fiduciary duties to former partners.
Yes, because any loss that reduces a retired partner's payments is a breach of loyalty.
Yes, because the retirement agreement makes Yuri a guarantor.
None of the above.
oe: Bane rejected that view.

Correct. Bane v. Ferguson (Posner, J.): a retired partner whose pension ended when the firm collapsed had no claim, because the managing partners owed no fiduciary duty to former partners, and the business judgment rule shields mere negligence.
Loyalty concerns conflicts and self-dealing, not losses from investment decisions.
Nothing suggests a guarantee.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Duties to former partners (Bane)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Prairie CPA Partners is a general partnership of five accountants governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Its managing partner, Yuri, invests the firm's $2,000,000 cash reserve in a bond fund after reading the fund's prospectus and consulting the firm's banker. The fund collapses, and the firm loses $1,200,000. Zoe, a partner who works at the firm's satellite office, asks to see the firm's books and the investment file. The partnership agreement provides: "A partner may inspect the books only with the managing partner's approval." Abe, a partner who retired two years ago and is paid under a retirement agreement, also wants to sue Yuri.

After the loss, the partners propose amending their agreement to add: "No partner shall be liable to the partnership for any act or omission, including intentional misconduct." Would that clause be fully enforceable?
o: No, because the agreement may not change the duty of care in any way.
Yes, as long as the clause is in writing.
No, because bad faith and intentional misconduct cannot be excused.
Yes, because partners may waive any duty they choose by unanimous amendment.
None of the above.
oe: The duty of care may be altered, just not eliminated or used to excuse bad faith or knowing misconduct.
Writing does not cure a term the statute forbids.
Correct. § 105(c). The agreement may alter the duty of care if not manifestly unreasonable, but it may not exonerate those kinds of conduct.
Some protections cannot be waived even unanimously.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Exculpation limits (§ 105)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Vela Restaurant Group hires Wes under a contract that calls him an "independent consultant" and lets either side end it on 30 days' notice. In practice Wes runs Vela's flagship restaurant: he sets the menu and prices, hires and fires staff, approves budgets, and signs checks on Vela's account. While running the restaurant, Wes secretly helps a celebrity chef plan a competing restaurant two blocks away, recruiting Vela's head chef and two of Vela's investors for it.

Wes argues that he owed Vela no fiduciary duties because his contract calls him an independent consultant. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Wes is not an agent, because the parties agreed in writing that he is an independent consultant.
Wes is not an agent, because Vela can end the contract on 30 days' notice.
Wes is an agent only for contracts he signs in writing.
The label does not control; Wes is likely an agent because of how the parties operated.
None of the above.
oe: Labels are informative but not decisive.
The power to end the relationship is consistent with agency, not against it.
Agency is not limited to written contracts.

Correct. MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff: agency turns on the parties' actual practices, including the right to control and the power to bind, not on what the contract calls the relationship (R3d § 1.02).
D is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Labels vs. practice (MJ & Partners)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Vela Restaurant Group hires Wes under a contract that calls him an "independent consultant" and lets either side end it on 30 days' notice. In practice Wes runs Vela's flagship restaurant: he sets the menu and prices, hires and fires staff, approves budgets, and signs checks on Vela's account. While running the restaurant, Wes secretly helps a celebrity chef plan a competing restaurant two blocks away, recruiting Vela's head chef and two of Vela's investors for it.

Did Wes breach a fiduciary duty by helping the competing restaurant?
o: Yes, because he helped a competitor and recruited Vela's people while still its agent.
No, because an agent may prepare to compete while still employed.
No, because the competing restaurant belonged to the chef, and Wes had no ownership stake in it.
No, unless Wes had signed a non-compete agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. An agent must not compete with the principal, or help others compete, during the agency (R3d § 8.04). Recruiting the principal's key employees and investors goes far beyond permitted preparation (MJ & Partners; Bancroft-Whitney).
Preparing to compete is allowed, but not recruiting the principal's people for a competitor during the agency.
Helping another compete is still a breach of loyalty.
The duty of loyalty exists without any contract clause.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Helping a competitor while still an agent

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Vela Restaurant Group hires Wes under a contract that calls him an "independent consultant" and lets either side end it on 30 days' notice. In practice Wes runs Vela's flagship restaurant: he sets the menu and prices, hires and fires staff, approves budgets, and signs checks on Vela's account. While running the restaurant, Wes secretly helps a celebrity chef plan a competing restaurant two blocks away, recruiting Vela's head chef and two of Vela's investors for it.

Before his scheme is discovered, Wes orders $30,000 of kitchen equipment for the flagship restaurant on Vela's account. Is Vela bound?
o: No, because Wes was only a consultant.
Yes, because buying equipment is incidental to running the restaurant.
No, because Wes was secretly disloyal to Vela when he placed the order.
Yes, but only if Vela ratifies the purchase.
None of the above.
oe: The label does not limit his authority; what Vela let him do does.

Correct. Implied actual authority covers acts incidental to the agent's express duties and supported by past practice. A supplier dealing with the manager of a restaurant could also rely on apparent authority from his position.
His breach elsewhere does not void an authorized contract with an innocent supplier.
No ratification is needed when the agent had actual authority.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Implied authority from the role

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Vela Restaurant Group hires Wes under a contract that calls him an "independent consultant" and lets either side end it on 30 days' notice. In practice Wes runs Vela's flagship restaurant: he sets the menu and prices, hires and fires staff, approves budgets, and signs checks on Vela's account. While running the restaurant, Wes secretly helps a celebrity chef plan a competing restaurant two blocks away, recruiting Vela's head chef and two of Vela's investors for it.

Why might Vela prefer to sue Wes for breach of fiduciary duty rather than for breach of his consulting contract?
o: A fiduciary claim cannot be brought against a consultant.
A fiduciary claim requires a written agreement.
Fiduciary claims are open-ended and can yield broader remedies, such as disgorgement.
Contract claims always yield larger recoveries, because they include expectation damages.
None of the above.
oe: Wes is an agent whatever the contract calls him.
Fiduciary duties arise from the agency relationship itself.

Correct. The course contrasts fiduciary and contract claims: a fiduciary breach may be easier to prove and yields broader remedies. Contract clauses (full-time duties, conflict disclosure, non-competes) can address the same risks in advance.
It is usually the reverse.
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Fiduciary vs. contract claims

q: In Lamkin v. Brooks, the town was vicariously liable for its police officer's attack on the plaintiff, but its insurer was not. Why?
o: The town's insurance policy excluded coverage for intentional acts.
Insurers are never liable for police misconduct.
The insurer was never notified of the claim.
The officer acted outside the scope of his employment when he attacked the plaintiff.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The attack was closely enough connected to the officer's police duties to be within the scope of employment, but the insurer's intentional-acts exclusion kept it off the hook.
There is no such rule.
Notice was not the basis.
If he had, the town would not have been vicariously liable either.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Lamkin v. Brooks

q: Which of the following is NOT an accurate statement about agency principles in a general partnership?
o: Each partner is a fiduciary of the partnership and the other partners.
A partner can bind the partnership only after the other partners approve each transaction.
Each partner is an agent of the partnership.
Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations, including those arising from co-partners' and employees' acts.
The partnership is liable for a partner's torts committed in the ordinary course of its business.
oe: Accurate (§ 409).

Correct: this statement is inaccurate. Each partner is an agent of the partnership, and a partner's act apparently carrying on the business in the ordinary course binds it without case-by-case approval (§ 301).
Accurate (§ 301).
Accurate (§ 306(a)).
Accurate (§ 305).
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Agency within a partnership

q: Wade and Xia are the only two partners in a RUPA partnership. Wade dies, and for the next 100 days Xia neither admits a new partner nor takes any other step. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership dissolved 30 days after Wade's death, when Xia had not admitted a new partner.
The partnership dissolved the moment Wade died.
Wade's estate automatically becomes a partner.
The partnership continues indefinitely as long as Xia keeps running the business.
None of the above.
oe: Wrong. The period in § 801(6) is 90 consecutive days, not 30.
Under RUPA, death dissociates a partner; it does not by itself dissolve the firm.
The estate succeeds only to Wade's transferable interest, not his status as a partner.
A partnership needs at least two partners; § 801(6) sets the deadline.
Correct. A partnership dissolves upon the passage of 90 consecutive days during which it does not have at least two partners (§ 801(6)). That happened here at day 90, a result none of A–D states.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — No second partner (§ 801(6))

q: Two equal partners want to avoid the problem illustrated by National Biscuit v. Stroud and Summers v. Dooley. Which provision in their partnership agreement would best address it?
o: A clause requiring the regular supplier's consent before either partner orders more goods.
No clause, because each partner already has a veto over the other.
A tie-breaker or decision-maker for disputed ordinary matters, or a buy-sell clause.
A clause requiring unanimous consent for every decision.
None of the above.
oe: Suppliers are not parties to the agreement.
A partner who is not a majority cannot veto an ordinary-course act as to third parties (Nabisco).

Correct. With two equal partners, neither is a majority: each can bind the firm to outsiders on ordinary matters (Nabisco), but neither can make the firm pay for a disputed decision internally (Summers). The course's advice is to agree on a tie-breaker or decision-maker, or a way out.
That makes the deadlock worse and does not bind third parties without notice.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Planning for deadlock

q: What best explains the different results in Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery and Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch?
o: Corroon & Black involved a partnership; Town & Country involved a corporation.
The former employees in Town & Country had signed non-compete agreements, while Hosch had not.
Hosch never solicited his former clients.
Town & Country's list was a costly trade secret; Corroon & Black's lists were widely known.
None of the above.
oe: Both are agency cases about departing employees.
Hosch's non-compete had expired; Town & Country did not turn on a non-compete either.
He did take clients with him; the issue was whether the lists were protected.

Correct. Town & Country's customers were found through costly cold calls, so the list was a trade secret and soliciting from it could be enjoined. In Corroon & Black the lists failed the six-factor trade-secret test, and insurance buyers shop around.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Town & Country vs. Corroon & Black

q: A buyout agreement requires the partnership to buy out any partner who becomes permanently disabled. Which funding source best matches that trigger?
o: Disability insurance.
A forced sale of the partnership's assets.
The disabled partner's 401(k) account.
Life insurance.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The course pairs each trigger with a funding source: death with life insurance, retirement with a pension or 401(k), and disability with disability insurance.
Avoiding a forced sale is one reason to have a funded buyout.
A retirement account funds retirement, and in any case belongs to the partner.
Life insurance funds a buyout triggered by death.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Funding a disability buyout

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kara, Leo, and Max plan to open a craft distillery. Max will invest $300,000 and wants no role in management and no personal liability. Kara and Leo will run the distillery full time, will contribute no money, and want to control the business. All three want to avoid entity-level income tax. They ask you which business form to use.

Suppose the three simply start the distillery together, sharing profits, without filing anything. What business form have they created?
o: Three sole proprietorships.
An LLC, because the parties want limited liability.
A general partnership, in which all three, including Max, are personally liable.
A limited partnership, with Max as the limited partner and Kara and Leo as general partners.
None of the above.
oe: They are carrying on one business together as co-owners.
An LLC requires filing a certificate of organization.

Correct. Co-owners carrying on a business for profit form a general partnership whether or not they intend to (RUPA § 202(a)), and every partner is personally liable (§ 306(a)). Max's wish to be passive does not shield him.
An LP exists only when a certificate is filed.
C is correct.

Q7–11 HYPO: Kara, Leo, and Max plan to open a craft distillery. Max will invest $300,000 and wants no role in management and no personal liability. Kara and Leo will run the distillery full time, will contribute no money, and want to control the business. All three want to avoid entity-level income tax. They ask you which business form to use.

Suppose they form a limited partnership, with Kara and Leo as general partners and Max as the only limited partner. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The LP must pay entity-level income tax.
Max is shielded, but Kara and Leo are personally liable.
Max loses his shield if he ever votes on a major decision.
All three are shielded from personal liability.
None of the above.
oe: An LP is a pass-through entity.
Correct. In an LP, general partners manage the business and have unlimited liability; limited partners risk only their investment.
ULPA (2001) § 303 largely eliminated the control rule.
General partners of an ordinary LP are personally liable.
B is correct.

Q7–11 HYPO: Kara, Leo, and Max plan to open a craft distillery. Max will invest $300,000 and wants no role in management and no personal liability. Kara and Leo will run the distillery full time, will contribute no money, and want to control the business. All three want to avoid entity-level income tax. They ask you which business form to use.

Kara and Leo like the LP structure but do not want to be personally liable for its debts. Which of the following would achieve that?
o: Forming a corporation owned by Kara and Leo to serve as the LP's only general partner.
Electing limited liability limited partnership (LLLP) status in the LP's certificate.
Filing a statement of qualification as a limited liability partnership (LLP).
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The corporate general partner bears the general partner's liability, and Kara and Leo act only as its officers (Frigidaire).
True. An LLLP shields its general partners too (ULPA §§ 102(10), 404(c)).
False. An LLP is a general partnership that elects limited liability; the LP version of that election is the LLLP.
Correct. A corporate general partner or LLLP status keeps the LP structure while shielding Kara and Leo.
C is wrong; an LP elects LLLP status, not LLP status.

Kara and Leo will run the distillery full time, will contribute no money, and want to control the business. All three want to avoid entity-level income tax. They ask you which business form to use.

Which of the following best describes a manager-managed LLC with Kara and Leo as managers and all three as members?
o: All three are shielded, pass-through tax treatment is kept, and Kara and Leo manage.
The LLC must pay entity-level income tax.
Max is shielded, but Kara and Leo are personally liable for the LLC's debts because they are managers.
Max will be able to bind the LLC to contracts, because every member is an agent.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. LLC members and managers are not personally liable for the LLC's debts solely by reason of their status (ULLCA § 304), the LLC is a pass-through entity, and a manager-managed structure puts management with the managers.
LLCs combine limited liability with pass-through taxation.
Managers of an LLC are shielded too.
A member is not an agent of the LLC solely by being a member (ULLCA § 301).
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — The LLC alternative

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kara, Leo, and Max plan to open a craft distillery. Max will invest $300,000 and wants no role in management and no personal liability. Kara and Leo will run the distillery full time, will contribute no money, and want to control the business. All three want to avoid entity-level income tax. They ask you which business form to use.

Suppose the three form a general partnership governed by the RUPA, agree to split profits equally, and say nothing about losses. The distillery fails and loses all of Max's $300,000; there are no outside debts. Under the RUPA's default rules, what do Kara and Leo owe Max?
o: Nothing, because they contributed only services.
$150,000 each, because they ran the business that lost the money.
$300,000 each, because partners are jointly and severally liable.
None of the above.
oe: That is the Kovacik v. Reed result, which the RUPA rejects.
Loss shares follow profit shares, not fault.
Joint and several liability runs to outside creditors; between partners, losses follow the loss shares.

Correct. Losses are shared in proportion to profit shares (§ 401(a)), and the RUPA's comment says this applies even to partners who contributed no capital. Each partner bears a third of the $300,000 capital loss, so Kara and Leo must each contribute $100,000 to repay Max's capital.
D is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Greer, a lawyer in solo practice, shares office space, a receptionist, and expenses with Hale, another lawyer. Each keeps his own clients and his own fees. The office door and their shared letterhead read "Greer & Hale, Attorneys at Law," and Hale knows it. Ivy hires Greer after reading the letterhead and believing that the two lawyers are a firm. Greer then commits malpractice in Ivy's case, and he has no insurance and no assets.

Are Greer and Hale partners in fact?
o: Yes, because their letterhead calls them a firm.
Probably not, because they share only expenses, not profits or a business.
Yes, because they share an office, a receptionist, and the costs of running the practice.
No, because lawyers may not form partnerships.
None of the above.
oe: The letterhead may create liability by estoppel, but it does not make them partners in fact.
Correct. A partnership requires carrying on a business as co-owners for profit (§ 202(a)). Sharing office expenses, without sharing profits or control of a common business, is not enough.
Sharing space and staff is cost sharing, not co-ownership of a business.
Lawyers form partnerships all the time.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Sharing expenses is not partnership

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Greer, a lawyer in solo practice, shares office space, a receptionist, and expenses with Hale, another lawyer. Each keeps his own clients and his own fees. The office door and their shared letterhead read "Greer & Hale, Attorneys at Law," and Hale knows it. Ivy hires Greer after reading the letterhead and believing that the two lawyers are a firm. Greer then commits malpractice in Ivy's case, and he has no insurance and no assets.

Can Ivy recover from Hale for Greer's malpractice?
o: No, because Hale is not actually Greer's partner and never shared in Greer's fees.
No, because Hale did not commit the malpractice.
Probably yes, because Hale consented to being held out as a partner and Ivy relied on it.
Yes, but only if Hale and Greer split their fees.
None of the above.
oe: Partnership by estoppel creates liability without a partnership in fact.
A purported partner is liable for the obligations of the purported partnership, not just his own acts.

Correct. A person who consents to being represented as a partner is liable, as if he were a partner, to one who relies on the representation in entering into a transaction with the purported partnership (§ 308(a)).
Fee splitting goes to whether they are partners in fact; estoppel rests on representation and reliance.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Liability as a purported partner

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Greer, a lawyer in solo practice, shares office space, a receptionist, and expenses with Hale, another lawyer. Each keeps his own clients and his own fees. The office door and their shared letterhead read "Greer & Hale, Attorneys at Law," and Hale knows it. Ivy hires Greer after reading the letterhead and believing that the two lawyers are a firm. Greer then commits malpractice in Ivy's case, and he has no insurance and no assets.

Which additional fact, if true, would most help Hale defend against Ivy's claim?
o: Hale has his own malpractice insurance.
Greer and Hale never signed a written partnership agreement with each other.
Hale never met Ivy or spoke with her about her case.
Ivy hired Greer on a friend's referral and never saw the door or letterhead.
None of the above.
oe: Insurance does not affect whether he is liable.
That shows they are not partners in fact, which is not the issue.
Personal contact is not required when the representation is made on the door and letterhead.

Correct. Without reliance on the representation there is no liability by estoppel. In Young v. Jones, the investors lost because they never saw or relied on any representation that the two Price Waterhouse firms were partners.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — No reliance (Young v. Jones)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Greer, a lawyer in solo practice, shares office space, a receptionist, and expenses with Hale, another lawyer. Each keeps his own clients and his own fees. The office door and their shared letterhead read "Greer & Hale, Attorneys at Law," and Hale knows it. Ivy hires Greer after reading the letterhead and believing that the two lawyers are a firm. Greer then commits malpractice in Ivy's case, and he has no insurance and no assets.

Greer also sends the "Greer & Hale" letterhead out in mass mailings to the public. Under RUPA § 308(a), how far does Hale's liability extend?
o: To anyone who relied on the public representation, even if Hale didn't know of it.
To every client of Greer's, whether or not the client relied.
To no one, because a mailing is not a representation.
Only to people whom Hale personally told that he was Greer's partner in the practice.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. If the representation is made in a public manner, the purported partner is liable to a person who relies on it even if the purported partner is not aware of its being made to that person.
Reliance is still required.
A letterhead mailed to the public is a classic public representation.
Public representations reach further.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Public representations

q: In A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc., which of the following was NOT among the facts the court relied on to find that Cargill controlled Warren?
o: Warren's use of drafts and forms printed with Cargill's name.
Cargill's daily criticism of Warren's finances and management, and its view that Warren needed "very strong paternal guidance."
Cargill owned a majority of Warren's stock.
Cargill's right of first refusal on Warren's grain.
Warren's inability to make capital improvements, pay dividends, or sell stock without Cargill's approval.
oe: One of the court's factors.
One of the court's factors.
Correct: this was not a fact in the case. Cargill was Warren's lender and main buyer, not its owner; that is why the case shows that agency can arise from a course of dealing.
One of the court's factors.
One of the court's factors.

q: Why did the court in Parker v. Domino's Pizza reverse summary judgment for the franchisor?
o: The driver was a Domino's employee on its payroll.
Domino's manual controlled nearly every detail of operations, so control was a jury question.
Franchisors are always vicariously liable for accidents caused by their franchisees' delivery drivers.
Domino's had ratified the driver's conduct by continuing to accept his deliveries.
None of the above.
oe: The driver worked for the franchisee.

Correct. The "veritable bible" of a manual covered recipes, delivery, hiring advice, and audits. Pervasive operational control can make a franchisor a principal, the counterpoint to Murphy v. Holiday Inns.
There is no such rule; the case turned on the degree of control.
Ratification was not the basis.
B is correct.

q: Under RUPA § 409(b)(3), a partner's duty to refrain from competing with the partnership:
o: Applies before the partnership dissolves.
Applies only if the partnership agreement contains a non-compete clause.
Continues for the rest of the partner's life.
Applies only to the managing partner.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The statute requires a partner to refrain from competing with the partnership in the conduct of its business before its dissolution. Other loyalty duties, such as accounting for benefits derived in winding up, continue during winding up (Monin v. Monin).
It is a statutory default that applies without any clause.
The no-compete duty is tied to the life of the partnership.
Every partner owes it.
A is correct.

q: Under Delaware's approach to limited partnership agreements, which of the following statements is true?
o: The agreement may eliminate default fiduciary duties, but not the implied covenant.
The general partner's fiduciary duties can never be modified by agreement.
The implied covenant lets courts rewrite unambiguous terms that they find unfair to investors.
Limited partners may never be bound by a conflicts committee's approval.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Delaware gives maximum effect to freedom of contract (Sonet; El Paso), but the implied covenant survives, and courts use it only to fill true gaps, not to rewrite clear terms (Cincinnati SMSA; Nemec).
Delaware lets the agreement restrict or eliminate them.
Courts will not use it to expand a precise term (Cincinnati SMSA).
El Paso enforced a conflicts-committee standard set by the agreement.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Delaware's contract-first approach

q: Which of the following statements about partnership finance terms is correct?
o: A partner may withdraw her capital contribution at any time on reasonable notice.
A draw is a distribution of profits; an advance is a loan repaid with interest.
By default each partner is paid a salary for her work.
Capital accounts are kept at market value.
None of the above.
oe: Capital is not returned before withdrawal or liquidation.
Correct. Draws are periodic profit distributions; advances (loans) are repaid with interest, unlike capital contributions.
By default partners receive no compensation for services, except for winding up.
They are kept at book value (cost), which is why book-value buyouts can pay so little.
B is correct.

q: Courts use the word "dissolution" loosely. As the course recommends, "dissolution" is best understood as:
o: The moment winding up is complete and the partnership ends.
Any partner's departure from the partnership, in every case.
The point when the firm stops operating as a going business and begins to wind up.
The partnership's sale of all of its assets to an outside buyer at the very end of winding up.
None of the above.
oe: That is termination.
That was the UPA's usage; under RUPA a departure is a dissociation, which may or may not lead to dissolution.
Correct. Courts have used the word for a partner's departure, for the winding-up process, and for its completion; the best usage marks the turn from running the business to winding it up.
A sale may be part of winding up but is not what dissolution means.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — What "dissolution" means

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ada, Bo, Cy, and Di are dentists who practice together as Smile Partners, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, or retires, the partnership "shall purchase" that partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account," payable in equal installments over five years without interest. The agreement says nothing about divorce or about a partner who simply wants to leave. The partnership's books carry its office building at its 1998 cost.

Cy dies. His estate argues that his interest should be valued at market value, because the office building has tripled in value and the practice has goodwill. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The estate gets market value, because the RUPA requires going-concern value in every buyout.
The clause is void, because book value is always unfair.
The estate may force a liquidation of the practice.
The estate likely gets only the capital-account balance, a book-value figure.
None of the above.
oe: The § 701 price is a default, and a buyout agreement may replace it.
Courts enforce such clauses; the lesson is to draft them carefully.
The agreement obligates the partnership to buy Cy's interest, and the estate cannot override it.

Correct. G & S Investments v. Belman: "capital account" meant the book figure, not market value, so the estate received very little. A capital account records contributions plus profits minus losses and draws at book value, so the building's appreciation and the goodwill are left out.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Capital account means book value

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ada, Bo, Cy, and Di are dentists who practice together as Smile Partners, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, or retires, the partnership "shall purchase" that partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account," payable in equal installments over five years without interest. The agreement says nothing about divorce or about a partner who simply wants to leave. The partnership's books carry its office building at its 1998 cost.

Cy's estate also argues that it is entitled to interest on the unpaid installments, as § 701 provides. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The estate is entitled to nothing until the partnership dissolves.
The estate is entitled to immediate payment in full.
The estate is entitled to interest, because § 701 cannot be varied.
The agreement likely controls, because § 701's rules are defaults.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement requires the partnership to buy the interest now.
The agreement provides for five years of installments.
§ 701 is not among the § 105(c) provisions that cannot be varied.
Correct. Nearly everything in RUPA's dissociation and buyout provisions is a default rule; the partners agreed on installments without interest.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Agreed payment terms

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ada, Bo, Cy, and Di are dentists who practice together as Smile Partners, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, or retires, the partnership "shall purchase" that partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account," payable in equal installments over five years without interest. The agreement says nothing about divorce or about a partner who simply wants to leave. The partnership's books carry its office building at its 1998 cost.

Di, who is not retiring, dying, or disabled, tells her partners that she is leaving to join another practice. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Di cannot leave until a buyout price is agreed.
The partnership must buy Di's interest at her capital-account balance.
Absent another provision, her withdrawal from this at-will partnership dissolves it.
Di's departure is wrongful, because the agreement does not list voluntary withdrawal as a trigger.
None of the above.
oe: She has the power to dissociate at any time.
The capital-account price applies only to the listed triggers.

Correct. The agreement covers only death, disability, and retirement. With no term and no other agreement, a partner's express will to withdraw from an at-will partnership causes dissolution and winding up (§ 801(1)).
Leaving an at-will partnership breaches no express term, so it is rightful (§ 602(b)).
C is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ada, Bo, Cy, and Di are dentists who practice together as Smile Partners, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, or retires, the partnership "shall purchase" that partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account," payable in equal installments over five years without interest. The agreement says nothing about divorce or about a partner who simply wants to leave. The partnership's books carry its office building at its 1998 cost.

The partners ask you to improve their buyout agreement. Which of the following changes would address weaknesses in it?
o: Adding triggers for divorce, voluntary withdrawal, bankruptcy, and seizure of an interest by a creditor.
Replacing the book-value price with an appraisal, a formula, or a price the partners agree on each year.
Protecting a departing partner against later claims for partnership debts.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The course's checklist lists all of these triggers.
True. These avoid the G & S problem of a stale book value.
True. Protection against partnership debts is on the drafting checklist.
Incomplete. Debt protection for the departing partner is also a recommended term.
Correct. Broader triggers, a realistic price, and protection against partnership debts all address gaps in this agreement.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ada, Bo, Cy, and Di are dentists who practice together as Smile Partners, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, or retires, the partnership "shall purchase" that partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account," payable in equal installments over five years without interest. The agreement says nothing about divorce or about a partner who simply wants to leave. The partnership's books carry its office building at its 1998 cost.

Bo retires. Over the years he contributed $60,000, was allocated $400,000 of profits and no losses, and took $430,000 in draws. Under the buyout agreement, what is Bo's price?
o: $0, because his draws exceeded his contributions.
A share of the building's current market value.
None of the above.
oe: Wrong. His draws ($430,000) were less than his contributions plus allocated profits ($460,000).
That leaves out the $430,000 in draws.
That is only his original contribution.
The agreement fixes the price at the capital-account balance.
Correct. Capital account = contributions + profits − losses − draws = $60,000 + $400,000 − $0 − $430,000 = $30,000, which is not among A–D.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Jada sues her former employer. At the mediation, Jada sits in the next room and confers with her lawyer, Kent, throughout the final round of talks. Kent tells the employer's lawyer several times, "I have authority to settle for $250,000," and signs a settlement for that amount. Before the mediation, Jada had privately told Kent not to accept less than $300,000. After the mediation, Jada refuses to honor the settlement.

Is the $250,000 settlement likely enforceable against Jada?
o: No, because Kent's private instructions set a $300,000 minimum.
Yes, because Jada's own conduct held Kent out as authorized.
No, because a lawyer never has authority to settle a client's case.
Yes, because Kent said he had authority.
None of the above.
oe: A private limit does not bind a third party who has no notice of it.

Correct. Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership: the clients attended the mediation, conferred with their lawyer during the final talks, and never limited his authority to the other side. Their conduct gave him apparent authority, so the settlement binds them.
A lawyer may have actual or apparent authority to settle.
An agent's own statements are not enough; it is Jada's conduct that supplies the manifestation.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ackerman: the client's conduct

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Jada sues her former employer. At the mediation, Jada sits in the next room and confers with her lawyer, Kent, throughout the final round of talks. Kent tells the employer's lawyer several times, "I have authority to settle for $250,000," and signs a settlement for that amount. Before the mediation, Jada had privately told Kent not to accept less than $300,000. After the mediation, Jada refuses to honor the settlement.

Which of the following statements reflects the holding in Ackerman?
o: Hiring a lawyer does not by itself give the lawyer apparent authority to settle.
A client is always bound by any settlement her lawyer signs.
A settlement binds a client only if she signs it herself.
Apparent authority requires that the agent correctly understood the instructions his client gave him.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The court found apparent authority in the clients' conduct at the mediation, not in the mere fact that they had hired a lawyer.
The court rejected so broad a rule.
The clients in Ackerman did not sign, and they were bound.
Apparent authority can bind the principal even if the agent misread his instructions.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Hiring a lawyer is not enough

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Jada sues her former employer. At the mediation, Jada sits in the next room and confers with her lawyer, Kent, throughout the final round of talks. Kent tells the employer's lawyer several times, "I have authority to settle for $250,000," and signs a settlement for that amount. Before the mediation, Jada had privately told Kent not to accept less than $300,000. After the mediation, Jada refuses to honor the settlement.

Which of the following statements is true?
o: Kent lacked actual authority to settle for $250,000.
Kent may be liable to Jada for any loss caused by his disregard of her instruction.
Jada may avoid the settlement because Kent misread her instructions.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Jada's instruction set a $300,000 floor.
True. An agent who acts beyond his actual authority is liable to the principal for the resulting loss.
False. In Ackerman, apparent authority bound the clients even if the lawyer misread his instructions.
Correct. Jada is bound to the employer, but she may look to Kent for her loss.
C is wrong; the agent's mistake does not undo apparent authority.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Jada sues her former employer. At the mediation, Jada sits in the next room and confers with her lawyer, Kent, throughout the final round of talks. Kent tells the employer's lawyer several times, "I have authority to settle for $250,000," and signs a settlement for that amount. Before the mediation, Jada had privately told Kent not to accept less than $300,000. After the mediation, Jada refuses to honor the settlement.

Before the mediation, the employer's lawyer had written to Kent that a pending $275,000 offer would expire at 5 p.m. that day. Kent never told Jada, and the offer lapsed. Jada argues that she never had notice of the deadline. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Notice to a lawyer is never notice to the client.
Jada is charged with notice only if Kent acted adversely to her.
Jada is not charged with notice, because Kent never passed it on.
Jada is charged with notice, because notice to her agent is notice to her.
None of the above.
oe: Lawyers are agents, and the ordinary rules apply.
Backwards: an agent acting adversely to the principal is the main exception to imputation (§ 5.04).
The rule exists so that third parties may deal through the agent.
Correct. Notice given to an agent authorized to receive it is notice to the principal (R3d § 5.02), and an agent's material knowledge is imputed to the principal (§ 5.03).
D is correct.

q: Which planning step would most likely have kept the teacher in Gorton v. Doty from being found to be the coach's principal?
o: Telling the coach to drive carefully.
Having the coach sign a note saying that he was not acting as her agent.
Lending the car outright, with no condition about who would drive.
Asking the school to pay her for the use of the car.
None of the above.
oe: Giving instructions is a form of control, which supports agency.
Labels do not decide agency.
Correct. The agency finding rested on her condition that only the coach drive, which supplied consent and control. The casebook's planning lesson: lend the car outright, or carry insurance.
Payment would make agency more likely, not less.
C is correct.

q: Under which theory does a principal's liability to a third party depend on the third party's detrimental change of position in reliance?
o: Estoppel.
Express actual authority.
Implied actual authority.
Ratification.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Estoppel requires the third party's justifiable, detrimental change of position, and it compensates the reliance loss (R3d § 2.05; Hoddeson).

The partnership may recover in full from Mia, because she alone was at fault for Pete's injuries.

The LLP filing does not shield partners from pre-filing obligations.

Q12–15 HYPO: Rowan signs an exclusive listing agreement with Quinn, a real estate broker, to sell his lake house for a 5% commission. Quinn finds a buyer, Sela. To avoid paying the commission, Rowan tells Sela to wait until the listing expires next month and then sells the house to her directly.

Which of the following best describes Rowan's duties to Quinn?
o: No duties at all, because the principal controls the agency.
Only the duty to pay the commission named in the contract.
Contractual duties of good faith, pay, reimbursement, and indemnity, but not fiduciary duties.
The same fiduciary duties of loyalty and care that Quinn owes to Rowan as his listing agent.
None of the above.
oe: The principal owes contractual duties.
The duties go beyond compensation.

Correct. A principal's duties to an agent are contractual, not fiduciary: the contract's terms plus good faith and fair dealing, reasonable compensation if contemplated, reimbursement, indemnity, cooperation, and non-interference (R3d §§ 8.13–8.15).

He tells Quinn to advertise in a regional magazine, which costs her $2,000, and to tell buyers that "the dock is brand new." Rowan knows the dock is twenty years old; Quinn does not. Quinn finds a buyer, Sela. To avoid paying the commission, Rowan tells Sela to wait until the listing expires next month and then sells the house to her directly.

Rowan delays the sale to Sela until after the listing expires so that he will not owe Quinn a commission. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Rowan did nothing wrong, because the sale closed after the listing expired.
Rowan likely breached his duty to deal with Quinn fairly and in good faith.
Rowan breached a fiduciary duty of loyalty that he owed Quinn.
Quinn may recover only if Sela also knew about the scheme.
None of the above.
oe: A scheme to time the sale around the listing defeats the very commission Quinn earned by finding Sela.
Correct. A principal must deal with the agent fairly and in good faith and may not frustrate the agent's earning of compensation (R3d §§ 8.13, 8.15).
The principal's duty is contractual good faith, not fiduciary loyalty.
Sela's knowledge is irrelevant to Rowan's duty to Quinn.
B is correct.

Must Rowan reimburse Quinn the $2,000 she spent on the magazine advertising?

Only if Quinn's advertising produced the buyer.
No, because the listing expired before the sale.
No, because a broker's advertising expenses are always covered by the commission she earns.

Rowan specifically directed this expense.

Q12–15 HYPO: Rowan signs an exclusive listing agreement with Quinn, a real estate broker, to sell his lake house for a 5% commission. He tells Quinn to advertise in a regional magazine, which costs her $2,000, and to tell buyers that "the dock is brand new." Rowan knows the dock is twenty years old; Quinn does not. Quinn finds a buyer, Sela. To avoid paying the commission, Rowan tells Sela to wait until the listing expires next month and then sells the house to her directly.

Sela sues Quinn for repeating the false statement about the dock. Which of the following statements is true?

Rowan breached his duty to Quinn by having her make a statement he knew to be false without warning her.
Quinn cannot be liable to Sela, because she was following instructions.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A principal must indemnify the agent for losses from carrying out the principal's instructions (R3d § 8.14).
True. A principal must deal fairly with the agent, including warning of risks the principal knows of (R3d § 8.15).
False. An agent remains liable for her own torts even when acting for a principal (R3d § 7.01), though she may have defenses, such as lack of knowledge, to particular claims.
Correct. Quinn has claims against Rowan for indemnity and for breach of his duty of fair dealing.

Custom or trade usage for the agent's position.
An emergency that requires the agent to act at once to protect the principal's property and interests.
Acts incidental to, or reasonably necessary for, the agent's express duties.
The principal's past acceptance of similar acts by the agent.

A source of implied authority.
A source of implied authority.
A source of implied authority.
A source, and among the most important (Mill Street Church).

The partnership may not sue a partner for breaching the partnership agreement.
A partner may sue another partner only after the partnership dissolves.

Suits may be brought while the partnership continues.

What is the effect of Ray's written notice under the RUPA?
o: Ray is dissociated, and Pat must buy his interest under Article 7 while the business continues.
Ray's withdrawal is wrongful, because he is leaving a profitable business.
Ray is dissociated, and because the partnership is at will, it dissolves and must be wound up.
Ray remains a partner until the assets are sold.
None of the above.

Leaving an at-will partnership is rightful unless it breaches an express term.
Correct. A partner's express will to withdraw from an at-will partnership dissolves it (§ 801(1)), and the partnership continues only to wind up.
He is dissociated when the partnership receives notice of his will to withdraw (§ 601(1)).
C is correct.

Pat's damages are measured by the difference between his winning bid and the value of what was left, $70,000.
Ray's fiduciary duties ended when he gave notice of his withdrawal.
A and B.
A, B and C.

False. Duties concerning the winding up continue; dissolution does not free a partner to take the firm's key asset.

Q7–11 HYPO: Pat and Ray, brothers, are equal partners in P&R Courier, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. The firm's most valuable asset is an exclusive delivery contract with MedLab, which can be assigned only with MedLab's approval. Ray gives Pat written notice that he is withdrawing. Meanwhile, Ray keeps his own application for the MedLab work pending. MedLab chooses Ray instead of Pat, and the firm's remaining assets are worth $20,000.

While the firm is winding up, Pat signs a new two-year delivery contract with a new client, Dynex, which does not know that the partnership has dissolved. Which of the following statements is true?

The firm may be bound to Dynex, but Pat lacked authority for new business and owes Ray any loss.
The partnership is bound, and Pat owes Ray nothing.
The contract is an act appropriate for winding up.
None of the above.

Correct. After dissolution a partner has no actual authority to start new business, but a partner's act binds the partnership if it would have bound it before dissolution and the other party lacks notice of the dissolution (§ 804). § 805 makes Pat liable for knowingly binding the firm to new business.

Pat argues that Ray, having caused the dissolution, may not take part in winding up the business. Which of the following statements is true?

Ray may not take part, because a dissociated partner never participates in winding up.
Ray may take part only with Pat's consent.
Only a court-appointed receiver may wind up the business.
None of the above.
oe: Wrong. No court approval is needed; § 802(c) gives him the right.
The bar applies only to a wrongful dissociator.
The statute gives Ray the right without Pat's consent.
The partners wind up the business; court supervision is optional (§ 802(e)).

Correct. A person whose dissociation resulted in dissolution may participate in winding up as if still a partner, unless the dissociation was wrongful (§ 802(c)). Ray's was not wrongful, so he may take part without anyone's approval, a result none of A–D states.

Yes, if Pat continues the business under a new name.
Yes, because Ray's withdrawal forfeited his interest.
No, because a partner may not use dissolution to take the business without paying his co-partner.
None of the above.

A rightful withdrawal forfeits nothing.

Correct. Page v. Page: the power to dissolve, like any fiduciary's power, must be used in good faith; a partner cannot freeze out a co-partner and keep the business without paying for it (followed in Second Measure v. Kim).

The provision is enforceable, because an LLC is a creature of contract.
The provision is enforceable as long as all members signed it.
The provision is unnecessary, because members of an LLC never owe fiduciary duties.

Unanimous consent does not cure a term the statute forbids.
Members of a member-managed LLC owe loyalty and care.
A is correct.

In proportion to contributions: $30,000 to Hana and $15,000 each to Ian and Joe.
As the majority of members decides at the time.

Without the others' consent, Ian signs a contract in Bramble's name to buy the neighboring 200-acre farm, a purchase far larger than anything the LLC has ever made. Which of the following statements is true?

None of the above.
oe: A member is not an agent of the LLC solely by being a member (§ 301), and in any case fundamental acts need everyone's consent.
A majority suffices only for ordinary-course matters.

Correct. In a member-managed LLC, ordinary matters are decided by a majority of the members, but acts outside the ordinary course and amendments to the operating agreement require the consent of all members (§ 407).
Management rights are per member, not per dollar, by default.
C is correct.

Q12–15 HYPO: Bramble Farms, LLC is a member-managed LLC formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Hana, Ian, and Joe. Hana contributed $100,000, and Ian and Joe contributed $50,000 each. The operating agreement provides: "No member owes any duty of loyalty to the Company or to the other members." It says nothing about distributions. The members have never held a formal meeting or kept minutes.

A creditor of Bramble Farms argues that the members are personally liable because the LLC never held a formal meeting or kept minutes. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Only Hana is liable, because she contributed the most.
The members are personally liable, because LLCs must hold annual meetings and keep minutes.
Ignoring formalities is not a ground for liability; the creditor would have to pierce the veil.
The members are liable up to twice their contributions.
None of the above.
oe: Contribution size has nothing to do with liability.
The ULLCA imposes no such requirement as a condition of the shield.

Correct. Under ULLCA § 304, members are not personally liable for the LLC's obligations solely by reason of their status, and failing to observe formalities is not a ground for imposing liability. Veil piercing is the main exception to the LLC shield.
There is no such rule.
C is correct.
